items.title: Yankees ride five-run first to series-opening romp of Diamondbacks
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
The two starting pitchers entered this game trending in opposite directions. Gerrit Cole had just allowed the most home runs (seven) in a two-start span in his career, while Eduardo Rodriguez is in the midst of a career year with a 2.62 ERA. One of those trends remained — Cole giving up another home run on a fastball — but fortunately the other trend was momentarily halted, the Yankees scoring five in the first off E-Rod to give themselves enough of a cushion to weather Cole’s continued home run woes.

Cole settled down after the Carroll dinger to give the Yankees six innings, by which time the offense all but put this game out of reach. They kept the pressure on, scoring a further four runs including solo home runs by Ben Rice and George Lombard Jr., to cruise to a series-opening victory in the desert, 9-2.

Rodriguez came into this game with an ERA above six in the first inning and an ERA right around two for the subsequent innings combined. That made it imperative that the Yankees find a way to do damage before the home team had a chance to come to bat, especially with the rate Cole is giving up the long ball. They did just that with a clear disciplined approach not to expand the zone against E-Rod’s curveball.

Paul Goldschmidt drew a leadoff walk, Cody Bellinger followed with a single, and Heliot Ramos also walked to load the bases with no outs. Rice drew the Yankees’ third walk in the first four batters to plate Goldschmidt and open the scoring, Goldy, Ramos, and Rice all working full counts before taking the free pass. Amed Rosario then fought off a cutter that handcuffed him up and in, muscling it to the opposite field perfectly between center and left fielder to plate Bellinger as the runners went station to station. A wild pitch allowed Ramos to score and Rice and Rosario to move up to second and third. This set up a two-run ground ball single from Lombard that just got by Geraldo Perdomo’s diving attempt to atone for his defensive misplay in the 13th that allowed the Twins to walk off the Yankees on Wednesday.

Rodriguez struck out Volpe to end the inning giving him three strikeouts in the frame, but the damage was done. The 45 pitches he threw were the most he’s thrown in the first inning in his career. Thirty-three of those pitches fell out of the zone, but only eight induced a chase.

It’s a good thing they hung such a crooked number, because Cole gave two of those runs back in the second. He gave up a leadoff single to Perdomo before yanking an 0-1 four-seamer right into Corbin Carroll’s nitro zone, the three-time All-Star obliterating it to right for a two-run bomb to reduce the Yankees’ lead, 5-2.

Rice made sure to immediately tilt the momentum back in his team’s favor. After falling behind 0-2, he stayed back on an elevated heater from E-Rod riding it out the other way and over the fence in left-center for a leadoff bomb, his 39th of the year, to give Cole some more of his cushion back, 6-2.

Cole settled down to work a scoreless third and fourth, helped in part by a sharp uptick in slider usage at the expense of some four-seamers as well as an impressive sliding catch in left-center by Spencer Jones in the third. He finally began dialing the fastball command to the corners in the fifth, striking out Tim Tawa and Lars Nootbaar on four-seamers to end the frame after Jesús Sánchez singled with one out. This allowed Lombard to restore the Yankees’ five run lead in the sixth, the rookie punishing a hanging curveball from E-Rod by lining the solo shot down the line it left and into the bullpen for his fourth of the year and third RBI on the night.

The four-seamer was the prime culprit for Cole in his previous two starts with a 68.2-percent hard-hit rate and just six whiffs, and that remained the case tonight. However, I believe it is Cole’s rustiness with his secondaries that is leading his four-seamer to get barreled. The fastball still has plenty of velocity — at 97 mph it’s a full tick above last season. I will grant that he has missed location in the zone on numerous occasions which hasn’t done him any favors.

However, after his last start, Cole identified a lack of chase and whiff against his secondaries as the reason his fastball is getting crushed. Hitters being able to lay off those chase pitches forces Cole to overuse the fastball in counts that favor the softer stuff, which in essence gives them the opportunity to hunt the heater when they should be defending against the breaker. When you can hunt a fastball in any count, chances are you are going to do damage when Cole misses his spot in the zone, the high velocity not much of a weapon when hitters’ bats are preemptively sped up.

Indeed, once he started commanding his slider and knuckle curve to the shadow of the zone in the middle innings, the hard contact against the fastball dried up. Having pitched a strong fifth and sixth and with his pitch count at 90, Boone saw no reason to overextend Cole and ended his night after six with his best innings freshest in mind. He finished night having pitched six innings, allowing two runs on four hits with no walks and six strikeouts.

Despite possessing one of the stingiest bullpens in baseball, the Diamondbacks decided that a five-run deficit in the seventh was too steep to justify using their high leverage arms. So, Zac Gallen made his first career relief appearance, the former All-Star in the midst of am injury-plagued, below-replacement-level campaign. He allowed a leadoff single to Goldschmidt and walked Ramos and Rice — again, both in full counts — to load the bases with one out. Aaron Boone sent out Ryan McMahon to pinch-hit for Rosario, and he hit a sharp grounder to first that Pavin Smith gloved but airmailed the underhand toss to Gallen covering first as all the runners were safe and a run scored on the error. Spencer Jones then appeared to ground into the inning-ending double play, but his hustle out of the box and down the line just beat the throw to pick up an RBI and make it 9-2.

Ryan Yarbrough pitched 1.1 innings in relief of Cole and worked himself into and out of trouble in the seventh. Arizona put runners on second and third as Nolan Arenado singled and Carroll doubled with one out. However, Yarbrough struck out Jose Fernandez and Tawa to strand the pair in scoring position. Rice smoked his fourth triple of the year in the ninth but was stranded at third by a McMahon strikeout. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil recorded the final five outs of the game to seal the win, 9-2. With the Rays having lost to the Red Sox earlier in the evening, the Yankees’ deficit is back to four games in the division, making that looming four-game set against Tampa in the Bronx even more high stakes.

Cam Schlittler looks to cement his AL Cy Young case tomorrow after Dylan Cease suffered his shortest start of the season on Friday. The Yankees ace will face off against Brandon Pfaadt with a slightly more reasonable game start time. First pitch is scheduled for 8:10 pm ET with the broadcast remaining on YES.

items.title: New York Yankees @ Arizona Diamondbacks: Gerrit Cole vs. Eduardo Rodriguez
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
The Yankees will be without Aaron Judge for at least ten days after he was placed on the IL with a right calf strain suffered in the first inning of the Yankees’ loss to the Twins on Wednesday. It is a potentially mortal blow to their last gasp effort to chase down the Rays in the division. Nonetheless, they found ways to score, especially toward the end of his months-long absence with a broken rib, and they’ll have to tap back into that starting with tonight’s opener against the Diamondbacks

Gerrit Cole has a point to prove after giving up seven home runs in his last two starts, the most he’s given up in a two-start stretch in his career. Hitters just aren’t chasing his secondary pitches out of the zone in two-strike counts, forcing Cole to become predictable going for strikeouts with in-zone four-seamers. Opponents are increasingly hunting the fastball in counts that should favor Cole, allowing them to barrel pitches they’d otherwise be late on if they had to respect his secondaries. In 20 starts, Cole is 8-9 with a 3.67 ERA (114 ERA+), 3.95 FIP, and 117 strikeouts in 115.1 innings.

The Yankees face old foe Eduardo Rodriguez, in the midst of a renaissance season in year three of the four-year, $80 million deal he signed with Arizona in free agency after posting an ERA north of five his first two years in the desert. He has made 25 appearances against the Yankees in his career, the bulk from his time with the Red Sox, pitching to a 3.80 ERA, 4.41 FIP, and 120:52 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 128 innings. Despite averaging just 92 mph, his four-seamer grades out as fourth-best in MLB because of the way he tunnels it with his changeup, cutter, and curveball. In 30 starts, the 33-year-old southpaw is 15-6 with a 2.62 ERA (160 ERA+), 3.74 FIP, and 135 strikeouts in 178.1 innings.

The Yankees try to fit as many righties into their Judge-less lineup against the lefty, which means Paul Goldschmidt leads off, Heliot Ramos bats third, and Rosario fifth. That being said, their two best hitters against a southpaw are lefties in their own right, Cody Bellinger and Spencer Jones proving that handedness is not the only factor in pitcher-hitter matchup success. The defense let them down multiple times in their extra-innings loss to the Twins and will need to be much sharper against an Arizona offense that’s among the best at putting the ball in play.

The Diamondbacks have just two hitters in their lineup (Pavin Smith and Tim Tawa) who are below league average for the season by wRC+. Gabriel Moreno has established himself as one of if not the best all-around catcher in MLB, with a 139 wRC+ and 5.0 fWAR. He’s surrounded by a decent amount of pop, Corbin Carroll, Ketel Marte, and Nolan Arenado each with over 20 home runs on the year.

items.title: Aaron Judge heading to the injured list with calf strain
items.author: Estevão Maximo
items.content:
Just days after his return from a lengthy absence, Aaron Judge is once again heading to the injured list, a heavy blow for a Yankees team with great postseason aspirations that relies on the presence of their star player. Although the news broke today, Judge will be officially placed on the IL on Saturday, leaving the Yankees short a healthy player for tonight’s matchup against the Diamondbacks.

There has been a heavy cloud in Yankee land ever since Judge left Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins in the sixth inning of an eventual 5-4 loss. Now, we know for sure that he is out for nearly the entire remainder of the season (Jon Heyman reports that he could be activated for Game 162).

According to Judge, he felt a problem in the first inning but initially decided to play through it before eventually leaving with right leg discomfort that’s been diagnosed as a calf strain. In the game, Judge struck out in both of his plate appearances before giving way to pinch-hitter Heliot Ramos, who took over in right.

Moving forward, it’s a glass-half-empty, half-full scenario; considering this injury is unrelated to his previous issue, it mostly depends on how you want to look at it. Clearly, it’s severe enough that, at the very least, the Yankees decided to err on the side of caution, removing their star hitter from the home stretch.

As far as Judge’s replacement on the roster is concerned, since the official IL placement will come on Saturday, the Yankees can’t announce who is coming up, but all expectations are that Max Schuemann will get the nod. The utility player formerly of the A’s last appeared in the bigs roughly a month ago, accumulating 87 plate appearances in 41 games off the bench for the Yankees this season with a pair of home runs.

items.title: Yankees Mailbag: Lining up for the postseason
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
Good afternoon everyone, it’s time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. Remember to send in your questions for our weekly call by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com.

If the Yankees lose the division, at whose feet might you lay the blame, without resorting to excuses such as… injuries, or lack of options at the trade deadline, or too high prices for options that available at the trade deadline, or even further back, last offseason?

The Rays have just been the better team in the regular season, is what it boils down to if you want to wave all of those other reasons off as just “excuses.” Frankly, with the team losing Aaron Judge after May and not getting him back until just recently, I’m amazed that they’ve held firmly onto the top Wild Card spot and have even been in a position to challenge for the division. But the team did punt away a handful of games over the summer due to their struggling offense and the Rays simply haven’t gone on as terrible a stretch, syncing up with the Yankees’ latest hot streak to prevent them from gaining any ground. If there’s any culprit to pin the blame on, collectively its the lineup as a whole — but sometimes you have to tip your cap and say that another team’s success is just legitimate this season, and at this point I’m not going to diminish the fact that the Rays are a contender that pulled ahead. It’s on the Yankees now to run the gauntlet that they couldn’t last year and beat them when it matters most, assuming that the standings don’t dramatically flip from their upcoming showdown in the Bronx.

In lining up the pitching for the post season, against Boston, it’s probably Schlittler, Fried, and Cole. How does the Tampa Bay series line up after that?

I agree that it will probably be Schlittler, Fried, and Cole should the Wild Card Round go to a third game, but worries have certainly crept in about Cole’s spot there. The ace is in need of a get-right game after his last two outings have seen seven long balls launched over the last 11.1 innings he’s pitched, and if that carries over into a third consecutive start that officially becomes a capital-c Concern. Cole’s one of the best pitchers in the sport still when he’s right, but the home run derbies he can spawn from time to time are his biggest weakness and an elimination game is the worst possible timing to throw a pitcher like that out there. Cole has insisted that it’s a visibility issue with his pitching that he can tweak rather than an injury concern, but time is of the essence with only a handful of starts remaining in the regular season.

The Yankees have another viable postseason starter in Carlos Rodón, who could also line up as their Game 1 starter for the ALDS should they advance similar to how they pitched Luis Gil against the Blue Jays to open last year’s Division Series. Rodón could instead be the Game 3 Wild Card starter if Cole continues to look like a gamble, letting Cole rest until the ALDS instead where they could let him set the table and potentially steal back home field advantage from Tampa. I doubt they’d do this though, for two reasons: one, the Yankees believe in Cole and so long as he’s not running three-plus homer games all the way to October then he’ll be penciled in there, and two running Rodón has its own risks right now as his fastball velocity has dipped in September. The Sox offense would probably get woken up more facing Los’ heater right now than they would Cole’s, and so the status quo seems the most beneficial, with the rotation resetting for Schlittler grabbing a potential Game 2.

A lot was seen this year of the potential of 18 year old center fielder Yostin Pena. He has shown hitting for average and power with excellent baserunning skills albeit in the lower minors. Is he a five tool prospect that can reach the Bronx in a few years? How excited are the Yankees’ player development personnel?

Pena turned a lot of heads with his performance down in Tampa this season after getting the promotion stateside following just 37 games in the Dominican Summer League. His bat stayed scorching, turning in a .941 OPS in 24 games with six homers and 10 steals. His discipline at the plate is still a little wild but that’s to be expected for the massive leap he’s made already, and he displayed an elite ability in several key facets of the game already. He’s also got a cannon of an arm, something that’ll play well in any portion of the outfield but would especially pair well with covering the deepest parts of Yankee Stadium’s center field should he make it to the majors. His trajectory is a complete unknown considering how quickly he appeared on the map in the first place — this could simply be the pace that he blazes through the minors and we could be talking about the possibility of seeing him a year or two from now, or he may get adjusted to as he faces older competition and take some more time. One thing for certain is that he’ll be gracing some top prospect rankings after the rise he’s had, and there’s potential for him to be the organization’s biggest name on the farm by the end of next season.

items.title: Mile High: Former RailRider Rumfield rocking in Colorado
items.author: Scott Walsh
items.content:
BRONX, N.Y. — From the time he was traded from the Philadelphia Phillies to the New York Yankees in November 2021, T.J. Rumfield dreamed of playing in Yankee Stadium. That dream became a reality last week.

However, it didn’t come in Yankees pinstripes. Rather, it was in Colorado Rockies purple and black.

“It’s a dream come true, to be honest with you,” Rumfield said prior to the Rockies’ three-game series against the Yankees on Sept. 8. “Any time you’re in Yankee Stadium, it’s just hallowed ground. Just kind of walking around, it’s kind of surreal, taking it all in. This is the big leagues to me, this is the show. It would just be nice to come up here and play some good games.”

The 26-year-old lefthanded first baseman was dealt in January by the Yankees to the Rockies for pitcher Angel Chivilli. The trade has been a win for Colorado. While Chivilli has spent a good portion of the season on the injured list, Rumfield is a candidate for National League Rookie of the Year. He ranks seventh in Major League Baseball (fifth in the NL) in batting with a .300 average. He has 155 hits in 146 games, including 29 doubles, three triples, 15 home runs and 69 RBIs. He is second in the NL (third in MLB) in on-base percentage at .392. Defensively, he leads the team and is tied for second among all first basemen with 10 defensive runs saved.

“He’s the man. He’s so good,” said Rockies outfielder Jake McCarthy, who himself is having a career season. “It’s insane that this is his first year in the big leagues. I feel like he’s so calm and collected, he’s obviously got a great eye. It just seems like the game is in slow motion for him. It’s been super fun to watch.”

Twice, in May and June, Rumfield was named NL Rookie of the Month. Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer believes Rumfield should be NL Rookie of the Year.

“Just look at the numbers,” Schaeffer said. “He’s been so great this year offensively, defensively as well. This is a both sides of the ball game and he’s done a great job from both sides.

“He’s handled the pressure in his first year exceptionally well. Every game, he plays with so much confidence. T.J.‘s a kid who can handle anything.”

Rumfield has been having fun this season and is honored to just be mentioned and considered for an award like NL Rookie of the Year. “It just makes me grateful for all the people I had coming up that helped me, especially in the Yankees organization,” he said. “They developed me into the player I am today. I’ve been able to run with this opportunity now because of the preparation and the things I’ve done before this.”

His father Toby was drafted in 1991 by the Cincinnati Reds and played 1,204 games in the minors over 12 seasons, including four at Triple-A.

Originally selected by the Phillies in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft, Rumfield was dealt with left-handed pitcher Joel Valdez to the Yankees for right-handed pitcher Nick Nelson and catcher Donny Sands. He worked his way up through the Yankees organization: High-A Hudson Valley in 2022; Double-A Somerset in 2023, where he earned a Rawlings MiLB Gold Glove; and Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre in 2024 and 2025.

In two seasons with the RailRiders, he batted .288 in 252 games (265-for-920) with 57 doubles, one triple, 31 home runs, 158 RBIs, 157 runs and 113 walks.

“Scranton was so much fun. Playing for (manager) Shelley (Duncan) and playing for that city, I feel like it was just a blessing,” Rumfield said. “To be able to even have the opportunity to play with the Yankees in Triple-A and to play every single day, not every young guy gets that opportunity. To be able to do that and then eventually catch the eye of somebody from another organization is kind of what you dream about. And then to be able to be in the big leagues now is awesome.”

McCarthy is a Scranton native, so he and Rumfield have been able to bond over that.

“He’ll be like, ‘I used to live by this grocery store,’ and I’m like, yeah, I know that (place),” McCarthy said. “It’s funny. I just feel like Scranton kind of takes on a new meaning when you tell someone you’re from there in professional baseball. I feel like at some point, someone’s probably made a pit stop there whether they played or came as a visitor.”

Unfortunately, with the Yankees already having a lefthanded-hitting first baseman with power in Ben Rice, Rumfield was expendable and traded for Chivilli. He was a nonroster invitee to Rockies spring training and wound up earning a spot on the team.

“I think everybody within the Yankees organization was happy for me,” Rumfield said. “I don’t know if they were sad to see me go or anything. But they were definitely excited for me and the opportunity and I’ve just ran with it from spring training on, just trying to make the team out of camo and I did. I just didn’t look back from there.”

Colorado has one of the worst records in the major leagues. But with Rumfield and other young players like Cole Carrigg and Zac Veen complementing veterans like McCarthy and Hunter Goodman, the future looks promising for the Rockies.

items.title: Tour de Luxembourg: Pepijn Reinderink holds off late-race chase to secure stage 3 breakaway victory
items.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
items.content:
Pepijn Reinderink (Soudal-QuickStep) surged from a decisive breakaway and held off a late-race chase to win solo on stage 3 of the Tour de Luxembourg.

Reinderink got away from his breakaway rivals with 7km remaining and held a slim lead all the way to the finish, crossing the line just one second ahead of runner-up Davide Piganzoli (Visma-Lease a Bike) and third-placed Thomas Gachignard (TotalEnergies), while his teammate Mattéo Vercher finished in fourth at four seconds back.

Piganzoli moved up four places in the overall classification and now leads the race by six seconds over Gachignard and nine seconds over Vercher.

Stage 3 of the Tour de Luxembourg was a challenging 179.6km route from Wiltz to Diekirch that included climbs over Um Knupp, Montée de Knaphoscheid, and again over Um Knupp before entering two finishing circuits with two climbs over Montée de Haemerich and Montée de Seitert, each before dropping to the finish in the city of Diekirch.

After winning the previous day's stage 2, Marijn van den Berg (EF Education-EasyPost) started in the overall race lead by just four seconds ahead of both Pierre Gautherat (Decathlon CMA CGM) and Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin-Premier Tech).

Multiple attacks in the first few kilometres of the race that caused splits among the peloton but it wasn't until 35km in that a large breakaway cleared the field that included Nils Politt (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Noah Ramsay (Alpecin-Premier Tech Development), Antoine L'Hote (Decathlon CMA CGM), Tao Geoghegan Hart (Lidl-Trek), Gil Gelders and Pepijn Reinderink (Soudal-QuickStep), Pietro Mattio (Visma-Lease a Bike), Pierre Thierry (TotalEnergies) and Leo Hayter (Modern Adventure Pro).

The breakaway continued to gain time en route toward the second ascent, Montée de Knaphoscheid, and still had 1:45 on the peloton as they reached the third climb, Um Knupp.

A chase group joined the first group to form a larger 19-rider breakaway that also included Igor Arrieta (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Aurélien Paret-Peintre (Decathlon CMA CGM), Sam Oomen (Lidl-Trek), Lukas Nerurkar (EF Education-EasyPost), Gauthier Servranckx (Soudal Quick-Step Devo), Tijmen Graat and Timo Kielich (Visma), Thomas Gachignard and Matteo Vercher (TotalEnergies), and Eike Behrens(Lotto Kern-Haus Outlet Montabaur).

And four more riders were chasing them at roughly one minute back, including Samuel Flórez (Modern Adventure Pro Cycling), Joshua Gudnitz and Sebastian Nielsen (Team ColoQuick), and Luc Wirtgen (Tudor Pro Cycling).

As the front group hit the circuit, however, it split apart over the Montée de Haemerich. Arrieta surged, bringing Reinderink with him, and the pair raced into the final lap with a small lead, while Gachignard bridged across on the Montée de Seitert, and Piganzoli surged across as well.

On the last climb over the Montée de Haemerich, Reinderink had enough left to attack again and, this time, open a small gap on a chasing Gachignard. However, he looked over his shoulder and saw Piganzoli and Vercher were in hot pursuit, with Arrieta, Oomen and Behrens just 10 seconds behind with just 3km to go.

Over the top, Reinderink crested seven seconds ahead of now-three chasers - Piganzoli, Gachignard and Vercher - and plummeted to the Diekirch finish line to take the victory.

items.title: MotoGP plans to introduce two qualifying sessions each weekend, following F1 model
Why KTM's Red Bull Ring advantage is looking particularly potent in 2026
What we learned at Red Bull and Verstappen's wild kart race
items.author: Megan Cantle
items.content:
There was just one question on everyone's lips at Silverstone on Wednesday evening: could Max Verstappen beat 100 karters when starting from the very back of the grid?

The answer, emphatically, was yes.

Max vs 100 was the latest in a long-line of incredible marketing stunts from Red Bull, bringing together athletes, creators and journalists to take on the four-time Formula 1 world champion. The catch? He'd be starting from 101st and would be tasked with picking off every single one of them around the extended karting track at Silverstone.

Opinions were mixed on whether he'd be able to do it, with Arvid Lindblad having put the two halves of the grid through their paces the day before. He'd had less time to do it in, but was beaten in the first race, leading people to question whether Verstappen - with twice as many competitors and plenty of opportunities for pile-ups and chaos - would get it done in time.

That line of questioning was rendered redundant when he passed 60-plus people on the opening lap, and went on to win the race in just 14 of the planned 30 laps, even with a slight excursion that might have raised some track-limits eyebrows in an F1 race.

Impressive as that was, what was really astonishing was how many moving parts were constantly at play during the lead-up and race day itself.

The 100 karters were made up of some who had never even sat in one before alongside drivers with some serious experience and speed. They were given proper training and acclimatisation time and, even if some of them were "bounced past" before they had even taken the first corner, they were all brought up to speed remarkably quickly to a safe and competent level.

Red Bull really made the most of the event, and it was clear from his post-race press conference that Verstappen had genuinely enjoyed himself. Karting is the purest form of racing and no matter how much F1 experience a driver has, you can tell they all enjoy returning to it. It was never 'gimmicky' even though there were 'gimmicks', with the newly created proximity chat proving a hit with both the audience and seemingly Verstappen himself. (An F1 introduction when?)

As part of a group of media invited to the event, it's hard to quite put into words how much fun it was. We had access to the host of karters, a chance to put some questions to driver-trainer extraordinaire Lindblad, plus dinner and a tour at Red Bull's MK7 campus. You could tell there was a lot of genuine care and thought put into all of the details and, given the amount of people involved, it was remarkable that everything ran so smoothly.

Some parties involved in the running of the event might have hoped the race would have lasted a little longer, but all that means is that they'll have to give it another go at some point in the future. Anyone up for Max vs 200?

items.title: All the dumb moments that make this title so much sweeter: Part I (1974-89)
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
We’re in the home stretch, folks.

September brings a bunch of things. School for many young people (it was personally August for me up in State College), the start of all forms of football, the stretch run of the MLB season, and the end of a hot summer.

For us here at P&T, all it means is that a new basketball season is right around the corner. Before you know it, training camp will commence in a matter of days, and the Knicks will take the floor for the first time as defending champs in the preseason on October 5.

It’s been an offseason of celebration, but also one of reflection. A reflection on the long journey to get here.

53 years is an extremely long time. As we count down the final weeks to the season opener on October 20, we begin a five-part series chronicling some of the dumbest games, moments, and decisions of the past 53 years that slowly made us all think this day would never come… until it did.

Part I will focus on the downfall of the 1970s dynasty that served as the organization’s standard-bearer, while poor front office decisions and injuries derailed any chance at a soft landing through the late 1980s. We’ll then gradually go through the 1990s in Part II, the dreadful 2000s in Part III, the turbulent 2010s in Part IV, and cap it off with the Leon Rose era in Part V.

The Downfall of the Golden Era Knicks (1974-80)

Every single championship-caliber operation has to disassemble. It’s a fact of life. Championship windows do not last forever, and teams will have to eventually say goodbye to players who shaped an entire generation.

Time and time again, teams are presented with the reality of either retaining these aging pieces into their sunsets and risking a prolonged stint at the bottom or making the difficult decisions to trade them as they exit their primes at the risk of angering everyone. This is going to happen to the very Knicks we love so much; it’s inevitable.

The reverberations of the highly successful early 1970s Knicks began not too long after that second championship.

Willis Reed, the captain and two-time Finals MVP, played just 19 games after the 1973 NBA Finals. He was only 31 years old, but a body that had slowly deteriorated over the last several years finally gave out. He played 15 of the first 22 games in 1973-74 before missing the next 56 games. The big man returned for the final four regular-season games and the postseason, but was a shell of himself due to a debilitating knee injury.

He’d refuse to undergo another procedure that June, calling it quits on his career. He’s one of many guys whose bodies failed him, and you often wonder what would’ve happened if he’d played in an era when athletes are healthier than ever because of advances in sports science.

Also retiring that offseason were Dave DeBusschere and Jerry Lucas. The former was still an All-Star and All-Defense recipient, but he hung them up ahead of his 34th birthday. Lucas was already diminished after his brilliant 1972 season and slowly fizzled out of the franchise’s plans by the end of the 1973-74 season.

Without Reed, DeBusschere, and Lucas, the Knicks finished 40-42 in 1974-75 and were swept in the first round by the Houston Rockets. They fell even further in the following seasons, failing to make the playoffs in consecutive seasons until the great Red Holzman was next out the door, stepping down in 1977.

Reed would replace him as head coach and lead the Knicks back to the playoffs in 1978, but soon into the following season, we learned why it’s never a good idea to hire franchise legends into leadership posts. The Captain was fired 14 games into the 1978-79 season and replaced with Holzman again, who’d serve another few seasons as the rest of the guard fizzled out.

A week before that 1977-78 season, Clyde Frazier was shipped to Cleveland for Jim Cleamons. A franchise icon was shipped out as his career faded for a journeyman, a move that still irks Clyde to this day. The final remnant of the Golden Era faded away in 1980, when Earl “The Pearl” Monroe retired at age 36 due to persistent knee injuries. One era of Knicks basketball was dead, but maybe it didn’t have to end that way.

Declining An Opportunity To Purchase Julius Erving’s Contract (1976)

You may recall this already being mentioned in my piece on the worst trades in Knicks history. This, of course, wasn’t a trade, but should’ve been. It’s hands-down the worst decision in franchise history.

When the Nets were among the teams chosen to join the NBA after the ABA merger in 1976, the Knicks demanded that they pay a fee of $4.8 million over 10 years for encroaching on their territorial rights, a request that was sustained by the NBA alongside their $3.2 million fee for joining the league. In total, the Nets had to come up with $8 million just to exist. That’s over $46 million combined in 2026 dollars.

That’s a of money for an NBA team in the 1970s, when franchises were commonly worth just seven figures, so the Nets were looking for any reason to not pay some of that cash, prompting them to make an extremely tough decision.

Dr. J made $350,000 during this time, but wanted a renegotiation. As such, the Nets were willing to offload his salary and offered him to the Knicks, then owned by the Graham Paige Corporation and ran by Eddie Donovan in the front office.

The Knicks said no. They chose a few million over a future Hall of Famer.

Philadelphia purchased Erving for $3 million, and the rest is history. The Knicks let a rival get the best incoming ABA talent available and watched him lead the Sixers to a championship in 1983 while spending over a decade as a top-five player in the game. That playoff appearance in 1978? Ended by Erving’s Sixers. As was the one in 1983.

If the Knicks make this move and look past the dollar signs, they’d suddenly pair the aging Frazier and Monroe with one of the greatest small forwards to ever play the game. They were gifted the soft landing that no aging dynasty gets, and just declined it for money.

Trading Maurice Lucas for Truck Robinson (1982)

Another one from the worst trades article, the Knicks traded the prime years of a pretty damn good player for an aging, regressing player at the same position in a one-for-one deal.

The New Jersey Nets sent them a 28-year-old Maurice Lucas as a form of compensation for signing Ray Williams in free agency in 1981. In his one year in New York, Lucas averaged 15.8 points and 11.3 rebounds while shooting 50.3% from the field. It was his best overall season since he was in Portland, but the Knicks never saw him as a long-term option, shipping him to Phoenix for Robinson one year later.

The deal made sense at the time, as he was even more productive than Lucas the season prior, but he hit a hard regression in his age-31 season in 1982-83 and only lasted two seasons in New York, flaming out by age 33. He would hear it from the fans, being nicknamed “Dump Truck” for his startling fall-off.

Meanwhile, Lucas made his fifth All-Star team in his first year in Phoenix as part of a second prime that slowly dissipated a few years later. While Lucas would only have 2-3 years of All-Star-level talent post-trade, it was a helluva lot better than Robinson.

Trading Away The Right To Pick Mark Price (1984)

This was actually something I had no idea about before researching this article, and it might be a bit nitpicky, but the Knicks missed out on a perfect point guard companion for Ewing to sign a role player in 1984.

The NBA was still in the free agent compensation era, so the Knicks had to pony up assets to sign Pat Cummings on June 27, 1984. Ultimately, it wasn’t much: just a 1985 third-round pick and a 1986 second-round pick. The way we view picks nowadays, it’s no biggie.

Except… they could’ve used one of those picks. The Knicks were bad in both of these seasons, but especially so in 1986, which handed the Mavericks the No. 25 pick in the 1986 NBA Draft, the top pick of the second round. They used that pick to select future four-time All-Star point guard Mark Price.

Price would ultimately be flipped for a 1989 2nd, which allowed him to spend the next decade as a big-time foe in the Eastern Conference with the Cavs. He had four top-10 MVP finishes, was an early 3-point innovator, and consistently dished out eight assists a game for his entire prime. Imagine if the Knicks had him at point guard alongside prime Ewing.

Cummings was no slouch for the Knicks, having his best season in New York with a young Ewing underneath him in 1984-85, but injuries cost him 80 total games over the next two seasons as he dwindled into a backup behind the franchise’s next star. Woof.

The Rise and Fall of Bernard King (1985)

Who’s the best Knick ever? I still lean toward Clyde Frazier for the two championships and the personality that he still radiates to this day, but there’s a case to be made for a few people. Patrick Ewing, Jalen Brunson, Willis Reed, etc. One name that’s mentioned as a great Knick, but never in GOAT convos, is Bernard King. What he does have a case for, however, is having the greatest peak in Knicks history.

Acquired for a damn good player in his own right (Micheal Ray Richardson), King got down-ballot MVP votes in 1983 while leading the Knicks to the playoffs in the first year under Hubie Brown. He leveled up his game in 1983-84, finishing runner-up in MVP voting to Larry Bird while single-handedly dragging the Knicks to Game 7 against the powerhouse Celtics in the second round. In 12 postseason games that year, he averaged 34.8 points per game.

He was, pound for pound, the best player in the world the following season. He’d have a few multi-week absences with minor injuries, but he entered late March 1985 averaging over 32 points a night, a mark that would lead the NBA and all of Knicks history. He was well on his way to competing for the first MVP award in franchise history, but it all came to a screeching halt when he blew out his knee against the Kansas City Kings on March 23.

Torn ACL. Torn meniscus. Thigh bone fracture. It was a gruesome injury, one that few (if any) players had ever come back from. Doctors thought his career was over, despite being in his athletic prime.

It was a gut punch for the Knicks, who were already in a horrible season with a 24-47 record when King got injured. It would result in the team drafting Ewing, the next great franchise star, but there was absolutely a world where Ewing would get to play with King, as the even lottery system likely sealed the Knicks’ fate the moment they missed the playoffs.

Bernard King was poised to be the Tommy John of ACL surgeries; however. He eventually returned two seasons later, but he didn’t look the same in six games to finish the 1986-87 season, prompting the Knicks to release him after the season. That was probably shortsighted, as he put together four really great years for the Washington Bullets immediately after.

The 1987 NBA Draft Fiasco (1986-87)

When I called Mark Price a big-time foe, it was at least partially facetious. He played on a good Cavs team for a long time, but the Knicks lagged behind the Cavs with their Ewing revival, and the two teams only squared off in the playoffs once: a Knicks sweep in 1995, as Price’s career wound down.

Scottie Pippen is an all-time Knicks foe. He might not be on the Mount Rushmore with Michael Jordan, Reggie Miller, and whatever other flavor of Knick killer you like (my picks are Haliburton and Alonzo Mourning), but he’s a Hall of Famer who routinely beat the Knicks’ butt. His lone playoff series as the lead option went New York’s way in 1994, but he served as the perfect wingman to MJ’s dominance across the 90s.

He could’ve been a Knick, you know.

On November 12, 1986, the Knicks swapped their first-round picks in 1987 with the Seattle SuperSonics to get Gerald Henderson, a former Celtic and father of the best player on the worst team in NBA history. A rebuilding Knicks team appreciated his consistency over 60 games through the rest of the season, but he was waived six games into the following season, exactly 367 days later.

That pick swap was pretty ill-advised considering the team had been among the NBA’s worst for a few years now, but they believed in their young star to help make tangible progress in 1987 along with a smattering of veterans, which included Jawann Oldham, who was acquired for a 1987 Denver first-round pick just two weeks earlier.

As you might’ve guessed, the Knicks sucked again in 1987, losing 58 games and receiving the No. 5 pick in the still-young lottery format. The Denver pick they traded? No. 8. They traded two top-10 picks for Gerald Henderson and Jawann Oldham, who combined to play six games for the team after that season. Great stuff from Gordon Stirling.

Pippen was selected by the SuperSonics at No. 5 overall, but was traded on draft night to the Bulls… for the 8th pick, a 1988 2nd, and a 1989 pick swap. In a cruel fate of irony, the two teams that got their top-10 picks from the Knicks in lopsided deals for crummy veterans engineered an all-time draft night swap, even if one side feels quite resentful about only getting Olden Polynice out of it. If the Knicks had just simply passed on Oldham, they could’ve the Bulls in this situation.

If they had kept both picks? Maybe instead of Polynice, they drafted Horace Grant (No. 10) or even… Reggie Miller (No. 11). Imagine that. You either could’ve taken the legs out of a future dynasty by taking Grant and Pippen from the Bulls or rewritten the 90s in a different way by taking Reggie.

Silver lining, they at least made a good pick with Mark Jackson at No. 18, but he was out the door by 1992.

Johnny Newman Can’t Force Game 7 (1989 Second Round)

A heartbreaking end to a game against the Bulls in the playoffs? If I had a nickel…

The Knicks won fewer than 30 games in three consecutive seasons from 1985-87, but broke through by sneaking into the postseason at 39-43 in 1988, even if it meant losing in four games to Larry Bird and the Celtics. The following year, the team leveled up even more as Ewing ascended to become one of the best players in basketball, finishing fourth in MVP voting. The Knicks won 52 games and rolled past the Charles Barkley Sixers in the first round to get their first crack at the new look Bulls.

A team they’d be very familiar with over the next decade, Chicago was still a few years off from the otherworldly dominance that made them all-time legends, but their success against the Knicks really began here. Jordan scored 34 in Game 1 to steal it at MSG, and while a big game from Ewing evened it at one game a piece, the Bulls took both at home to push the Knicks to the brink. After winning Game 5, one objective remained. Steal Game 6 in Chicago and get a chance to close it out at the Mecca.

It was dead even in the first half, but Chicago had opened up a seven-point lead after three quarters. Into the final minute, it seemed firmly in their grasp. Leading by four with nine seconds left, the Bulls just needed to play smart on defense, make free throws, and they’d win it. That didn’t go to plan, as the Knicks got a gift from the heavens when Trent Tucker buried a three with six seconds left and was fouled, tying the game on a four-point play.

On the other end, Jordan drew a foul on a mid-range jumper with four seconds left, sinking both free throws and ending his day with 40 points. On the ensuing inbound, some atrocious full-court defense from the Bulls gave Johnny Newman, a 33.8% shooter from distance (a solid mark at the time), a wide-open three in transition to win the game and force Game 7.

He missed it. Bulls win. The season is over.

As many of us know, this would only be the start of the heartbreak that the GOAT and his Bulls would inflict on the orange and blue.

Rick Pitino’s Resignation (1989)

A decade that began with the final light fading from the Golden Age of Knicks basketball ended with a light at the end of the tunnel. Ewing, Jackson, and Charles Oakley were at the forefront of the next era of basketball in New York.

And they had done it with a 37-year-old born-and-bred New Yorker at the helm. Rick Pitino made the NCAA Tournament with Boston University in the early-80s, spent two years under Hubie Brown on the Knicks’ coaching staff, and led an upstart Providence bunch to the Final Four in 1987 before landing his dream job: head coach of the New York Knicks.

His first two years represented progress and the burgeoning of a new force in the Eastern Conference. He was young, the team was young, what could go wrong?

What went wrong is that Pitino handed in his letter of resignation on May 30, 1989, just 11 days after the season ended in Chicago, to return to the college game and coach Kentucky.

A season of optimism to end a turbulent decade ended with a big question: why would Coach Pitino leave? Especially for a college team in Kentucky’s situation. Once a collegiate powerhouse, the program was in utter shambles after receiving NCAA sanctions impermissable payment to recruits and entrance exam fraud. They weren’t even postseason eligible for the next two seasons! Any rebuild would take way longer; who would sign up for this with a great NBA job?

As has unfortunately been the case all too often in franchise history, it was a case of dysfunction.

Pitino and Knicks general manager Al Bianchi hated each other. When Pitino flirted with the Kentucky job that May, something that would admittedly irk any executive, Bianchi showed no intent to keep him. Pitino would later say that the relationship had reached a boiling point, and that he would end up taking the Kentucky job because he couldn’t coexist with Bianchi.

In a twist of fate, Bianchi would be canned just two years later by Hollywood producer and new president of Paramount (who oversaw the Knicks), Stanley Jaffe, who allegedly tried to talk Pitino out of visiting Kentucky in 1989 on behalf of ownership (then Gulf and Western) by telling him, “You need to trust me”. Pitino would later say that, had he known Jaffe would be taking over the franchise shortly, he wouldn’t have taken the Kentucky job.

The delay in said move caused the disastrous tenure of Stu Jackson over the next two seasons that saw the franchise move backwards. When the house was cleaned in 1991, the Knicks ultimately came out on top by getting Pat Riley to elevate them to the next level.

But, as we’ve come to know over these past 53 years, stupid moments like having your head coach on a 52-win team go back to college for a program that got sanctioned to hell is just the tip of the iceberg.

items.title: UCI bans former coach at women's Continental team for 10 years for aggressive language, acts of humiliation and intimidation
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Demko, who worked at the team until they stopped at the end of the 2025 season, was found to have breached article 5 (general principles) and article 6.4 (protection of physical and mental integrity) of the UCI Code of Ethics.

The decision also included 'aggravating circumstances' regarding article 2.1 (psychological abuse) and article 2.6 (minors and other dependent persons) of the code.

The breaches include aggressive, disrespectful, and demeaning language as well as acts of acts of isolation, humiliation, intimidation, and infantilisation towards a rider.

Demko has been banned from 'taking part in any cycling-related activity organised by the UCI or any of its affiliates' for 10 years, the UCI announced, while he has also been handed an unspecified fine.

"The UCI acknowledges the courage of the individuals who came forward in this matter, and recalls that any form of harassment or abuse is incompatible with the values of cycling," the UCI said in a statement.

The investigation into Demko came about as a result of several complaints submitted to the UCI Ethics Commission from several former staff members at Hess "concerning professional misconduct", as well as a rider "formerly coached by Mr Demko and with whom he had a consensual personal relationship and with whom he cohabited, concerning allegations of harassment and psychological abuse".

Several complaints were received via the UCI SpeakUp platform, a method for anyone involved in cycling to confidentially report abuse, harassment, misconduct, and other integrity issues.

The UCI Ethics Commission found that Demko habitually used aggressive and disrespectful language while working, and had demeaned the physical appearance of riders. The Commission also concluded that Demko had been abusive towards a rider he had coached, including acts of isolation, humiliation, intimidation and infantilisation.

"Based on the elements brought to its attention, the Commission concluded that Mr Demko’s conduct towards the riders and staff of the team – in particular the habitual use of aggressive and disrespectful language in the working environment, the unsafe and intimidating driving of team vehicles, and demeaning remarks concerning the physical appearance of staff and riders – had fallen short of the standards of integrity, care and diligence required of persons bound by the UCI Code of Ethics, and had involved an abuse of the position he held within the team," the UCI statement read.

"The Commission further concluded that Mr Demko’s conduct towards the athlete he coached had involved acts of isolation – including requests to sever contact with persons she trusted, the dictation of the content of her messages to them, and a threatening message addressed to her psychologist –, humiliation by way of public denigration on social media, intimidation – including threats to disclose personal information and a threat directed against a person she trusted –, and infantilisation.

"These acts, which persisted after the end of their relationship, had the effect of diminishing her sense of identity, dignity and self-worth. The fact that the above conduct arose within a consensual personal relationship between two adults did not remove it from the scope of the UCI Code of Ethics, given the coaching and dependent relationship between Mr Demko and the rider."

Hess Cycling raced from 2023 to 2025 with the aim of becoming Britain's first Women's WorldTour team. However, the team collapsed last year, owing thousands of pounds to riders, business partners, and suppliers, according to .

items.title: Tour of Slovakia: Lennert Van Eetvelt wins hilly stage 3 and takes over race lead
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Stage 3 of the Tour of Slovakia delivered a rare sight for the race as a rider not named Paul Magnier took victory.

A tough day through the hills with 2,100 metres of climbing on the road to Dohňany saw the final climb of the day – Kohútka (6.2km at 6.6%) - decide the stage as Lennert Van Eetvelt (Lotto-Intermarché) and Henrique Bravo (Soudal-QuickStep) broke clear at the front 25km from the line.

The pair left other attackers, including Simon Carr (Cofidis) behind, but were caught by a host of chasers in the final kilometres of the 195km stage as the group swelled to 28 riders.

Van Eetvelt and Bravo raced to the line together with their new companions, and it was Van Eetvelt who prevailed in the final sprint to the line. The Belgian beat Benjamin Thomas (Cofidis) and Valentin Hofer (Bahrain Victorious Development Team) to win the stage.

Van Eetvelt now takes over the race lead from Magnier, who won the first two stages but finished stage 3 minutes down. He leads the GC by four seconds from Thomas.

items.title: Tim Merlier edges Dylan Groenewegen to win Kampioenschap van Vlaanderen
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) outsprinted Dylan Groenewegen (Unibet Rose Rockets) to win Kampioenschap van Vlaanderen for a second time in two years. Uno-X Mobility's Søren Wærenskjold completed the podium as the top sprinters put on a show for the shootout in Koolscamp.

The fastman from Soudal notched his 11th victory of the season and held off a charge from his Dutch rival on the far right side of the road. Groenewegen now has five runner-up spots at the Belgian race, last winning in 2018.

On the final 500 metres, Unibet Rose Rockets lined up with three riders to lead out their sprinter up the middle. However, Merlier found an opening on the far right and swooped past with 100 metres to go.

"The headwind made things difficult, and you had to pick the right moment to go, but also have some luck to launch your sprint. I’m happy to take the victory here for the second time in my career, especially as it’s close to my home," Merlier said in a team statement after the victory.

"It’s a success that motivates me for the following races I have between now and the end of the season, in October.

Friday's 180.2km escapade was a 12-lap circuit around Koolskamp in West Flanders. Kampioenschap van Vlaanderen, also known as Koolscamp Koers, is the first in a trio of Belgian races for the weekend, followed Saturday by the Flandrien 0.0 Classic and Sunday by Gooikse Pijl.

For the opener, each circuit covered close to 17km, and was flat the entire way. Last year's winner Jonathan Milan was not present, which opened a huge opportunity for the rest of the previous podium, Groenewegen and Merlier, both former winners. Back after a year's absence was Philipsen, a winner in 2023.

Seven riders jumped away after 22km, and they opened a gap of 2:30 across the next two circuits. In the group were Alex Kirsch (Cofidis), Alexys Brunel (TotalEnergies), Born De Bobbelaere (VolkerWessels), Victor Vercouillie (Flanders-Baloise), Rokas Adomaitis (Energus Cycling), Guillaume Visser (EEW-VDK Cycling) and Gaetan Warnier (Dovy Keukens-FCC Cycling).

Once the break approached the start of the ninth lap, six remained with the margin cut in half; De Bobbelaere dropped. Another lap later and Adomaitis and Brunel faded from the front. The peloton began to stretch out into a single line, driven by Alpecin-Premier Tech.

The four riders remaining at the front carried only a 24-second advantage with two-and-a-half laps to go, 40km. Alpecin, Groupama, Soudal-QuickStep and Unibet Rose Rockets riders sensed it was time to make the catch as they moved to the front, but a trio resisted at the front.

Movement through crosswinds saw Kirsch, Warnier and Vercouillie holding a slim lead as several attacks from behind failed. Once on the bell lap, the sprint teams had made their catch to settle accounts in a traditional bunch finish.

From Pittem, with a direct line of 4km to go, Lidl-Trek and Uno-X Mobility positioned at the front of the peloton with the blowing directly headon. With 1 km to go, it was Unibet Rose Rockets taking over the pace, but they could not hold off the red-hot Merlier.

items.title: Wind tunnel tested: Who makes the fastest deep aero wide gravel wheels?
items.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
items.content:
Cast your minds back a decade and you'll be met with a world in which gravel bikes were barely out of diapers/nappies (delete as appropriate).

Gravel racing was nothing more than a flannel-coated subsection of cyclo-cross with a side order of IPA, and the concept of 'optimisation' was derided by all involved, for it was "against the 'spirit of gravel'".

Returning to the present time, the only is the ghost of that former sport, which has been killed off in favour of aero tubes, deep wheels, wide tyres, skinsuits and maximised carb intakes.

Money talks, so as prize money has grown, competition has become more intense, average speeds have rocketed, and the sport's laissez-faire approach has all but been replaced with a performance engineering mindset.

Nothing evidences modern gravel racing as clearly as the cohort of aero gravel wheels that have launched in the past few years.

It's well known that wider tyres roll more smoothly over rough terrain, but chunky tyres are naturally less aerodynamic; largely by dint of simply being bigger. So designers face the paradox of making gravel wheels that can house as wide a tyre as possible, while also trying to make them as aerodynamic as possible. Oh, and don't make them too heavy either! I don't envy their task.

The result is wheels like Zipp's 303 XPLR SW, Enve's G SES 6.7 and Black Inc's Sixty Four Gravel. All are as deep as their roadgoing counterparts, but designed to house what are essentially - and often literally - mountain bike tyres.

But which of those – and the others listed below – is winning the technical arms race? To find out, we headed to our second home: the wind tunnel.

We tested eight of the most race-focussed wheelsets we could get our hands on, all of which centre around wide internal rim beds, optimisation for wider tyres, and deep profiles.

The list, and accompanying gallery, is as follows:

  • Black Inc Sixty Four Gravel

Protocols and standardisations

As with our previous aero testing, we used the renowned cycling wind tunnel at Silverstone Sports Engineering Hub. Alongside aerodynamic drag calculations, we also weighed each wheelset, and measured the tyre widths to complement the aero data.

For the aero testing, every wheelset was mounted to the exact same gravel bike: the new, slightly wild-looking Factor Elara. We selected the Elara for two reasons: Firstly, the simple one is that we were already taking the bike with us on the day to test its own aero credentials. You can see how it did in our Factor Elara wind tunnel results write-up. Secondly, it made sense as it is the most unashamedly high-performance aero gravel race bike to launch this year. If any bike was a fitting mule for these hyper aero wheels, it was this. And no, Factor didn't pay me to say any of that.

To keep our data as precise as possible, we opted for a bike-only configuration rather than using a live rider. The variance in human body movement during a test sweep introduces a margin of error larger than the wattage differences expected between top-tier wheelsets. Removing the rider from the equation allows us to confidently attribute any performance deltas strictly to the wheels themselves.

To quantify our error margin on the day, which was also spent testing road and gravel bikes against our baseline Trek Emonda, we ran said baseline through a series of repeated runs, some at the start of the day, then more at the end.

In this case, the confidence margin we found was a CdA of 0.0004, or 0.2 watts at 35km/h.

To explain this with an example: If two tests of an identical setup measure differently, and said delta is 0.2 watts, then our confidence in the accuracy of any of the other tests cannot be any better than +/- 0.2 watts. And thus, if one wheelset measures at 99.8 watts, and another is 100.2 watts, they are statistically equal.

Testing was conducted at a wind speed of 35km/h, with the tunnel’s powered rollers spinning the wheels at the same speed. The crankset was fixed in a horizontal position with the driveside arm forward for all tests, with a small velcro strap holding the non-driveside crank arm in place on the nearby chainstay.

Every wheelset was fitted with the exact same pair of Vittoria Terreno Dry 55mm (2.2in) tyres, and we were careful to maintain the same front and rear orientation when swapping from wheelset to wheelset, to eliminate differences in manufacturing tolerances between individual tyres.

Brake rotors were removed and a SRAM Red cassette were transferred between wheelsets too, to avoid any potential unwanted interference on the results there.

All other things were kept identical, including the gear the bike was put into, the bottles on the bike, and even the pressure in the tyres (which was set to the recommendation provided by the SRAM Tyre Pressure calculator, which fluctuated slightly based on the internal width of the wheel).

Yaw sweeps and data capture

We tested each wheelset across seven distinct yaw angles: -15°, -10°, -5°, 0°, +5°, +10°, and +15°. For an idea of what that looks like, check out my above, aka the GIF of a bike transitioning between each yaw point.

Data was measured using 15-second static captures at each yaw point, and the sweep was always done in the same direction (negative to positive yaw) to maintain maximum repeatability.

There are a few caveats to throw into the mix before we get into the results.

Firstly, Black Inc. is owned by Factor, and so there's a possibility they were advantaged by our decision to test using the Factor Elara bike, as the two may have been designed in conjunction with each another. There's no knowing to what extent, if at all, this affected the results, and it is an issue we would have run into had we used a Crux (with Rovals) or a Revolt (with Cadex wheels).

Secondly, by testing without a rider on the bike, we aren't giving an accurate real-world representation of how the wheels will be challenged in their actual use. Both Specialized and Giant, for example, design and validate their with a pedalling-leg mannequin, and that when the turbulent air of a rider's legs is introduced, it's likely that their comparative performances will improve. The performance of the Tarmac SL8 in our road bike wind tunnel testing adds weight to this claim; without a rider it's mid-table, but with a rider aboard, it climbs to a much higher place in our rankings.

Thirdly, aero data should only be a small part of your buying decision when it comes to choosing the right wheels for you. Weight, price, build quality, customer service and many other factors are important too.

To get the results below, for each bike I averaged out the datapoints from each of the seven yaw angles.

In calculating those averages, I applied weightings in line with the 2018 research paper by Nathan Barry - A New Method for Analysing the Effect of Environmental Wind on Real World Aerodynamic Performance in Cycling - which weights each yaw angles to better reflect how often you'll experience it in real-world riding scenarios.

That average is then used to calculate the power required to overcome the aerodynamic drag.

Given we're measuring a bike without a rider, the actual wattages shown will be lower than you'll be used to seeing on your head unit, but remember it's the differences between each wheelset that we're interested in here, not the absolute values.

Ahead of publishing this writeup, I shared the data with each brand and gave them the opportunity to comment on the results. I will stitch in their comments below as naturally as I can.

Getting straight into the results, the fastest wheels on test were the Black Inc. Sixty Four Gravel, which come in at $2,399.00 / £2,199.00. They boast a 30mm internal width, a 40.25mm external width, a hooked bead, and as the name suggests, a 64mm deep rim profile.

This is followed closely by the Enve G SES Pro 6.7, which boasts the widest internal diameter here at 35mm. They use a hookless bead, like the Zipp and Hunt wheels below, and claim an external width of 42.6mm. The rear wheel is the deepest on test at 67mm, although the front is a smidge shallower at 60mm. At $3,100.00 / £3,500.00 for a pair, they're among the spendiest here too.

In third place is a product that's yet to be released from British brand Hunt, but which we were given exclusive early access to test, and I've been given explicit pre-embargo permission to tell the subscribers about. They're called the Hunt 5AM Gravel, or 5AMG for short. They are a 'reverse mullet' wheelset, with a 54mm front wheel and 49mm rear. They offer a 27mm internal width, with a hookless bead, and the front wheel boasts a chunky 45mm external width to help the airflow off the front tyre. I don't yet have prices on these.

Hunt's aero expert, Paddy Brown, who kindly loaned both their own wheels and the Zipp wheels to us for the test, said "we’re incredibly proud of how the 5AMG Ti_UD performed in this test. To come out near the top aerodynamically while also being one of the lightest wheelsets tested is a strong validation of the development work that has gone into this platform. The very wide front rim profile delivers real aerodynamic efficiency, while the Aero Mullet concept continues to prove its value beyond the road and into gravel."

Speaking of aero mullets, interestingly, Hunt and Roval – the Terra Aero CLX – landed the exact same result. They were separated by just one one-thousandth of a watt, but given our error margin is two-tenths, they're all but equal.

The Terra Aero CLX also offers a 27mm internal width with this reverse mullet concept, but Specialized introduces a 'chopped aero' design which squares off the trailing edge of the front rim, claiming equal aero performance to a deeper wheel, but with much less weight. The external width is also much smaller, at 38.5mm (38.4mm for the rear). Priced at $3,398.00 / £2,998.00, these are up there with the Enve and Cadex on price.

Below this comes Zipp, still only 1.9 watts behind the Black Inc wheels, with the the 303 XPLR SW – the wheelset that I think it's safe to say kicked off this whole aero wide gravel wheel game – with their 54mm depth, 32mm internal rim width (hookless), and 40mm external width. At $2,200.00 / £1,600.00, their price is relatively good in this company, and given they're a couple of years old now, it's not too difficult to find them on offer either.

Next up comes Cadex, with the Max GXR, which aren't quite as deep as the above counterparts, but still peddle the aero and wide marketing speak, despite a comparatively narrow 25mm internal width and 35mm external width. Their weight is impressive, as we'll get to below, but their $4,000.00 / £3,500.00 price tag is the spiciest here.

Bringing up the rear are a couple of wheels that have a different purpose. Their marketing isn't centred on being aero, but vibration absorbent.

First up, the Scribe Gravel Ultras are laced with Berd's polymer spokes, which are essentially string but possess an insane strength to weight ratio, while remaining flexy enough to swallow some of the bumps you feel on the road. Their 30mm internal width is among the widest even here, but the use of a hooked bead will perhaps swing the odds in their favour among some buyers. At $1,999.00 / £1,449.00, they're also the most affordable on test.

And finally, the Gulo GGA 44 also offers a hooked 30mm internal rim, but rather than using third-party Berd spokes, they come with a proprietary carbon spoke designed by Gulo itself. At $2,345.00 (approx £1,750.00, based on a currency conversion, but they're not sold in the UK), they're reasonably priced in this company, but neither their wind tunnel result nor their weight (seen below) will win them any custom.

Looking at the comparative weights of each wheelset, there's a fairly clear inversion of the results above. The more aero a wheelset is, the heavier it tends to be. Zipp and Gulo are slight outliers here, with their aero deficits not being made up on the scales.

Elsewhere, choosing between Roval and Hunt remains a difficult task, and Cadex shines as the potential hillclimber's wheelset.

Despite our Terreno Dry tyres being labeled as 55mm, on all of the wheels here, they blew up to less than 55mm when measured on our calipers.

A slight admission to this section is that we didn't remember to measure all of them (no conspiracy here, just a busy day and things sometimes get missed). I almost didn't include it as a result, but I decided to just share what we had, so those we did get are listed below. The widest was the Enve wheel, at 54.9mm, whereas the narrowest was 51.0mm, courtesy of the Cadex wheels. Naturally, there's a bit of correlation between the rim width and the tyre width.

Conclusions and takeaways

My first takeaway here is that there are definitely aero savings to be had in gravel, as we found in our , even with chunky 55mm rubber. That big tyre isn't ruining all the aerodynamic intentions of the wheels, and there's a strong correlation between wheel depth and aero performance. It's always reassuring to know these brands know what they're doing!

I'm aware not all of us will be riding at average speeds of 35km/h (I know I won't be at my current fitness), but for the points in races that matter, such as chasing back onto a group after a crash (ask me how I know), or bridging up to a breakaway where speeds are likely above your all-day average, there are aero savings to be taken advantage of.

But weight is still important. The way Specialized marketed the Crux 5 was notable – and logical to my mind. It said that aero is important, but given rolling resistance matters significantly more in gravel than it does on the road, and that rolling resistance scales with mass, weight should factor more heavily in a consumer's buying decisions for gravel than it does on the road.

Also… I don't know about your local gravel races but all of the ones I've done have been really damn hilly!

As a result, although the big hitters from Black Inc and Enve sit at the top of the table as the most aero on test, don't discount the Roval and Hunt wheels. They sit in a nice sweetspot that trades a watt of aero drag for around 350g of mass. How that equates to speed depends on the course you're riding, and your power output (because more power = more speed = a higher relative importance of aerodynamics).

One of the biggest takeaways for me, though, is that the gap between the aero wheels and the two 'comfort' focussed wheels is only around five watts. If you're racing flat gravel time trials, go all-in on aero, but if your usual gravel routes or race courses are bumpier, slower, and/or you'll spend your time riding in the relative shelter of a group, the lack of a big aero deficit in this dataset could actually sway you away from the Enve or Black Inc wheels in favour of the bump-smoothing comfort of Gulo or Scribe.

The one datapoint we don't have, however, is rolling resistance. Would a Berd spoke actually save more than five watts over rough ground or not? Or would the wider measured width of the tyre on the Enve wheels offset this? These are all things a wind tunnel won't tell you.

Still, I hope the data the wind tunnel can tell you – i.e., all that's written above – is useful. Thanks as ever for reading.

items.title: MotoGP Austrian GP: Who made Q2 - and who missed out
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Pedro Acosta continued to command KTM and Red Bull's home MotoGP race as he led throughout the Austrian Grand Prix Friday afternoon practice session too.

Gresini Ducati rider Fermin Aldeguer ended up his closest challenger, 0.127 seconds adrift.

Ai Ogura marked his return to the field after hand surgery by being top Aprilia in an impressive third place for Trackhouse.

None of the title contenders showed especially standout pace, though Marc Marquez brought his Ducati up to fourth by the end, just ahead of Jorge Martin's Aprilia.

Martin's team-mate Marco Bezzecchi had a particularly muted Friday, bar some errors under braking, and was only ninth.

The session was interrupted by a late red flag for a nasty crash for Alex Marquez.

His Gresini Ducati's front wheel locked as it hit the ground from a small wheelie out of the first corner, firing him into a crash that sent him sliding down the straight while his bike cartwheeled down the grass.

Marquez was able to rejoin on his spare bike after the restart and earned a Q2 place in eighth, just behind an unusually strong late-2026 performance from outgoing KTM rider Brad Binder.

Yamaha will be represented in Q2 thanks to Fabio Quartararo taking 10th place.

But Honda missed out despite LCR's Johann Zarco spending much of the afternoon in the top 10.

Zarco had an early crash at Turn 4 in which team-mate Diogo Moreira also went through the gravel while he was walking away. The stewards quickly determined that Moreira had had no time to react so had not breached yellow flag rules.

The LCR pair were edged down to 12th and 13th at the end, just behind works Honda rider Luca Marini.

items.title: KTM CEO reveals Acosta's key Marquez stance for 2027
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
KTM CEO Gottfried Neumeister says there was no financial offer that KTM could have made to tempt Pedro Acosta to stay, because Acosta is desperate to measure himself against Marc Marquez.

Though Acosta is yet to win a grand prix, he and Marquez are the two arguable standouts of the current campaign - with Marquez now the title favourite despite injury troubles and Acosta massively outperforming his KTM peers.

Acosta agreed a deal to replace Pecco Bagnaia at Ducati in the last off-season - despite the widespread belief that he could have commanded more lucrative contracts elsewhere.

KTM motorsport boss Pit Beirer said last weekend that KTM felt "there was somehow a chance" to kept him - "but also it was quite long growing in him that he wanted to go there and have the same bike as Marc, and just find out who is better, him or Marc, so there's something I think we couldn't even beat".

And this was corroborated emphatically by Neumeister during KTM's home MotoGP weekend at the Red Bull Ring, when he was asked by The Race about the damage losing Acosta does to his brand's championship ambitions in the short-term in MotoGP.

Neumeister was very keen to emphasise his faith in KTM's future factory line-up of Alex Marquez and Fabio Di Giannantonio - also making a point to specifically mention it after the end of his media session.

But of Acosta leaving, he said: "I'm really very sorry, and I tried. And it's not a secret. I tried personally to convince him to stay.

"But I mean, I still have goosebumps because he told me, 'Listen, Gottfried, it's not about a million more or less'.

"We have seen riders who are sitting on the best bike at the beginning of the season just signing with others for money. This is, for me, not a racing spirit, yeah?

"And he simply said: 'I'm Spanish. Even if you have a better bike, the 850cc, and I'd be winning on this one, I want to beat Marc with the same weapon.'

"And then you're disarmed, you're dismantled. And this is such a great encouragement. And I will always have the best feelings when I see him."

The line about 'signing with others for money' can be read as reference to joint-championship leader Jorge Martin - who had left KTM on bad terms half a decade ago and who this year committed to a switch from Aprilia to Yamaha early on.

All the evidence corroborates Neumeister's suggestion that KTM's relationship with Acosta remains very healthy until their end-of-year separation - with Acosta allowed to again test KTM's 850cc prototype this Monday at the Red Bull Ring (he already tested it at Brno) and Neumeister making reference to a potential reunion down the line.
