items.title: Campagnolo Bora X Wheelset review: A wonderfully balanced gravel race wheelset
items.author: andy@atpperformance.uk (Andy Turner)
items.content:
£1,999 / $2,810 / €2,290

1,463g/51.6oz (actual with valves and lockrings), 1,430g/50.44oz (claimed)

27mm internal, 31.5mm external

As Campagnolo expands its gravel range and revitalises the entire Super Record groupset to include off-road electronic Super Record X, it brings with it a new gravel-focused iteration of the famous Bora wheels, the Bora X. The brand claims the new wheelset brings the best out of the new groupset, and vice versa, due to the synergy between components.

I can’t comment on that, having not tested the new Super Record X groupset, but after a lot of riding on the Bora X wheelset, I can confirm that it is a highly competent wheelset in many ways.

It’s lightweight for a 50mm deep wheel, although it is a little on the narrow side by some standards meaning it is perhaps better suited for 40-45mm tyres rather than larger. However, the greatest performance aspect of these wheels is the balance of stiffness. Lateral and torsional stiffness are easy enough to achieve, but to manage that with vertical compliance for a comfortable ride is sublime for gravel riding.

A hoard of high-quality parts, bags and accoutrements boost the value of these wheels, although they are still a shade under two grand. The cup and cone bearing system is perhaps not the preference for most, it works well if you look after it. Not to mention, the wheels frankly look stunning. They are a real winner in my books and a perfect addition to any gravel race bike.

Design and specifications

The Campagnolo Bora X wheels are built upon a unidirectional carbon rim that very closely resembles the Bora WTO rims used on the road. The 50mm depth is high for a gravel wheel, and closely on trend with the increasing focus on aerodynamics in the discipline. The width of the rim is where the changes are bigger, with a 27mm internal channel designed for 35mm tyres and larger, using hooked rims still giving some riders that added sense of security. Externally, the rim reaches 31.5mm wide, relatively narrow by some standards in today’s market.

The rim also features a solid rim bed, eliminating the need for tubeless tape, with spokes instead adjusted externally. Valves are supplied and are long enough for the 50mm depth, which is designed to make tubeless setup very easy time after time. A glorious gloss C Lux finish is present on the rims, offset with a mix of matte black and chrome logos, which personally makes this a stunning set of wheels.

Moving down from the rim, the spokes are laced in the iconic G3 lacing pattern. This uses sets of three spokes, one on the non-drive side at the rear and the non-rotor side at the front, two on the drive-side rear and rotor-side front. This results in a 2:1 ratio 21-spoke lacing configuration, with the seven radially laced, and the 14 using a three-cross arrangement. The spokes themselves are straight pull and bladed, but not all of them, some are rounded to balance stiffness and comfort for gravel riding.

The freehub is available for all standards from Campagnolo, SRAM, and Shimano, and uses NSW ceramic bearings, rather than the top-end CULT offering, with cup and cone rather than cartridge bearings. This requires a bit more maintenance, but if looked after, should last well. Lightweight lockrings are supplied as standard and attach externally. A nice bonus is the supply of both tyre levers and soft padded wheel bags large enough for wheels with 50mm tyres fitted. Claimed weight is 1,430g, but actual was 1,463g, although with lockrings and valves. Remove those, and the wheels still come in at 1,444g.

Tubeless setup for these wheels was one of the easiest I've done. The solid rim bed means no rim tape is required, just fit the valves, put the tyres on, and inflate with a track pump to seat. The Panaracer GravelKing ZX 45mm tyres inflated to 45mm exactly on these rims with the 27mm internal width and 31.5mm external. This is a bit narrow by some gravel wheelset standards, especially by modern wider trends, but it allows the versatility to run 35mm and upwards.

I have to say that the wheels look glorious. The C Lux finish combines a gloss carbon weave across the entirety of the rim with a mix of matte black ‘Bora’ logos with a chrome-finished ‘Campagnolo’ and winged wheel nut logo. They reflect the light in the sun and really make the frame pop. They do lose this once the dust from gravel riding gets them, but they’re easy enough to clean. I personally prefer this a lot to the standard matte black that is now all too common.

Of course, these are performance gravel wheels, and they are an impressively balanced set which have several features that really help them on gravel. The spoke lacing is heavily asymmetric, with a 2:1 ratio on the rear drive side and front rotor side to better deal with the asymmetric forces applied to the wheels. This results in the wheels having a superb level of lateral stiffness for out of the saddle accelerations and putting the power down, but also a great deal of torsional stiffness when accelerating and braking.

Impressively, this is balanced with a good amount of vertical compliance which gives them a more plush sensation when riding off road on rougher surfaces. Some of this is apparently to do with the carbon layup, but also the use of elliptical spokes alongside the bladed aero ones. Of course tyres and pressures make up a lot of the cushioning sensation you get, which is why I test with the same tyres and pressures on the same routes to keep things consistent. The Bora X, however, are noticeably more comfortable to ride than other gravel wheels on test with all other variables kept consistent.

A 50mm depth means these are a solid set of wheels when travelling at speed. At speeds around 35kph the wheels start to come alive. I’ve used these on the road a few times as well, and even on faster group rides the wheels feel pretty at home and not much of a compromise compared to road wheels with 30mm tyres.

Impressively, with this rim depth, the weight is competitive. Excluding the valves and lockrings, 1,444g for a 50mm wheelset is impressively lightweight. This is felt out on the trails when accelerating on steeper inclines. This, with the stiffness, means they get up to speed very competently and also brake effectively even on loose surfaces with heavier tyres fitted.

There are some concerns about the longevity of the bearings, however, as a cup and cone setup requires more user input to keep them running smoothly, but if you do this, they will run very well. Generally, cartridge bearings would be used with heavier external seals and potentially internal as well. A ratchet system is still used, but a 36-tooth engagement is on the lower side of teeth numbers. However it is sometimes seen as more resilient than high-tooth ratchets, and in practice the acceleration of the wheels was great even with a lower tooth count.

These wheels are also potentially a little on the narrow side. 27mm internal width works well for 35-45mm tyres, and can be used for wider. However, for using 50-55mm options, as is becoming more frequent, a lot of wheels are adopting a wider internal and external width. Meanwhile, the 31.5mm external width does mean the 45mm tyres used with this sit fairly wide. We’ve seen in wind tunnel testing that although wider tyres carry an aero penalty, this penalty can be reduced if the external width of the tyre is wider to better smooth the interface between tyre and rim. I can confirm that riding on tarmac surfaces, the likes of the Parcours FKT felt to roll a bit faster above 35kph, with a ballooning 40mm maximum external rim width.

£1,999.99/$2,180 is an expensive set of wheels, putting it in the similar regions of the HUNT Limitless 40 UD Spoke with carbon rims, lower weight, and ceramic bearings. Of course, they are far behind the price of the likes of the Roval Terra Aero CLX (£2,998/$3,400) and the ENVE G SES 6.7 Pro (£3,500/$3,100).

My personal feeling with these wheels is that the versatility they offer is impressive. I like the inclusion of hooked rims, and with some 35mm tyres these would be great wheels on rough road surfaces let alone gravel. There is also no user weight limit, and a solid rim bed which makes future tubeless fitting a lot easier as tape won’t come loose while cleaning out old sealant.

Of course there are wheels that are cheaper, and not far off in terms of many performance aspects. The Scope R4G (£1,498/$1,798), for example, are superb, but the hub is like a siren while the Bora X are silent. Meanwhile, the Parcours FKT (£1,249 ) are great when rolling fast, but lack the same stiffness, compliance, and low weight that the Bora X offer.

I am also a big fan of the inclusion of the very lightweight external rotor lockrings, as well as the valves, tyre levers, bag for all of that, and some very high-quality wheel bags. It does mean that the wheelset as a whole does come with some additional value.

There is also the subjective element that I think these wheels look stunning, and that does add value to me. I like to look at the bike and think to myself that it looks great, and these wheels genuinely add to that. This is, of course, a highly individual and personal preference, but as are most aspects of value.

The Campagnolo Bora X wheels have become my favourite gravel wheelset to ride. The balance of high stiffness for accelerations, braking, and cornering, combined with vertical compliance for comfort is fantastic. A deep rim depth and low weight also makes them wonderful to ride at speed or on climbs.

My only gripe is the relatively narrow rim width for tyres beyond 40mm, while the bearing setup will require more upkeep. But for the performance and included parts, not to mention looking stunning, the £2k price tag does not appear too high. There are better-value (around £1,500) wheelsets, but I prefer these.

These are stunning wheels, they have turned heads and had plenty of longing attention. You have to keep them clean, but they look fantastic. Supplied spares and bags are also brilliant so you can ride them straight out the box with sealant, groupset components, and tyres.

A solid rim bed means no issues of tape leakages, and the valves supplied work well. It results in a faultless tubeless setup not just the first time, but every time after that.

What impresses me most with these wheels is the lateral and torsional stiffness, combined with the vertical compliance. It’s a very impressive balance to achieve and makes these superb gravel race wheels. The only area lacking a little is the width for tyres of 45mm and up. Otherwise, it’s hard to fault the system, and the silent freehub is something I love.

1,463g for a 50mm deep wheelset with hooked rims is good, even by road standards, especially at this price and without carbon spokes. Some of that low weight comes from being relatively narrower than some recent gravel wheelsets, and they are not the lightest, but a very strong competitor.

For a penny under £2k, I think these offer pretty good value. The inclusion of all required bits and bobs plus wheel bags adds to that value, and although Hunt does the same, I prefer the performance of these wheels. But £500 extra is still a high amount compared to some strong competitors, so although arguably better value than the £2.5+k wheelsets, the ~£1400 region of the market is potentially slightly better value.

items.title: 'No unrealistic expectations or unnecessary limitations' - Kate Courtney is diving head-first into the unknown
items.author: Dan Challis
items.content:
Ominous cloud formations gather over the Cumbrian market town of Penrith in late August, where the FDJ United-SUEZ team are staying ahead of the 2026 Tour of Britain Women. Temperatures are more than twenty degrees cooler here than the peloton has experienced throughout the summer while racing in mainland Europe as autumn draws nearer in northern England.

There is a sense of transition in the air in more ways than one as sits down with the team’s new signing, Kate Courtney, on the eve of her WorldTour debut. The American has been thrust into a new world, having left behind the XCO mountain bike circuit, and is about to find out for the first time whether she can match some of the best road racers on the planet on Britain’s rolling terrain.

"So many things have happened in such a short period of time that it actually makes it feel like it's been longer than it has been," Courtney says, reflecting on a whirlwind few months. "But looking back, it really has been quite accelerated, and I'm just really excited to be here."

"There were a lot of quick moves and decisions that had to be made in order to get me to the start line. Knowing that I get to line up this week, it's all worth that."

Courtney is one of the USA’s best-known racers and has been among the world’s top mountain bikers for almost a decade, winning the XCO world title in 2018. Just 97 days before the Tour of Britain, she lined up in her first UCI road race in Czechia in a bid to test out a possible career switch from fat tyres to thin ones.

Her potential was immediately confirmed, winning a hilly final stage at the UCI 2.2 level Tour de Feminin in Krásná Lípa. Even before that achievement, Courtney reveals that she had already been negotiating a full-time switch to road racing, with a home Olympic Games in Los Angeles a particular target in two years’ time.

"I'd had a lot of conversations prior even to that race in Czechia - which is a bit crazy that even before racing I knew that that's a jump that I wanted to make - and started to explore the opportunities," Courtney says.

"The FDJ opportunity actually came about before Nationals and was a really exciting opportunity that was a bit non-standard, I would say, but was one that just seemed like the perfect fit and was worth doing a lot to pursue."

"A lot of things are changing very quickly and all at once, but it's also a long process, and it's really nice to have what I would call a head start this year to start to dial in everything from bike fit to where I might base next season in Europe, and to have a bit of a head start in knowing what I'm going to need to be both successful but also happy in a whole new environment and world chasing this new dream."

The multi-disciplinary phenomenon in professional cycling is becoming more and more common, with many riders now encouraged to take up different disciplines from a young age. More seldom is Courtney’s case, as a rider who has excelled in one discipline transitioning into another where she has almost zero experience.

Ahead of May’s Tour de Feminin in Czechia, Courtney had only raced a few times on the road among the amateur peloton. Road racing in UCI events, and certainly in the WorldTour, was entirely new.

"When I was racing in Czechia, the goal was to really experience the European peloton and see how I felt within that environment and determine whether I loved learning in that environment," she says.

"When I knew I loved the racing and most of all I loved learning all the intricacies of road, I felt really confident committing to this path. What I'm committing to really is a long process of learning and experimentation and being thrown in the deep end and figuring it out."

There is a great deal that sets road racing apart from the mountain bike scene. The speed, racing tactics and bumping shoulders with competitors are elements that Courtney needs to excel in if she is to succeed. Racing in Czechia was an eye-opener.

"It was really overwhelming at first for me," Courtney says, describing her first UCI road racing experience. "I think for anyone who jumps into a 170-person bunch for the first time, it's just so many new stimuli that it's hard to relax a bit.

"I think for me a lot of this has been about finding the places that my skill set transfers, so I think once I got through that first day I started to realise that my bike handling transfers; positioning is not all that different than in a short track or in a super competitive World Cup mountain bike race, and I've been doing that since I was a kid.

"So finding the confidence that I can bridge the gap where my skill set is lacking, but also rely on a decade of racing experience. I think that's part of the process right now, just getting comfortable and getting confident with that skill set and applying it to an entirely new sport."

At the Tour of Britain, Courtney’s education took another leap. Her 11th-place finish in the overall classification and fourth on the penultimate stage to Hay-on-Wye revealed without doubt that she has the legs to compete at this level.

She would, however, be involved in an unusual uphill crash on stage 4, crossing wheels with her teammate Lauren Dickson as she led the peloton on a steep ascent. Described as "an unfortunate touch of wheels" by Dickson afterwards, whether it was just bad luck or inexperience showing through, the incident can be notched as another lesson learned.

"I'm totally not afraid of her bike handling skills or her feeling of riding in the bunch. I think it will be fine. For her, it's just getting to learn the peloton, the level," FDJ United-SUEZ sports director Lars Boom told ahead of the race. "It's a WorldTour race. There's some really strong riders. And it's just a quest for her to see what she can do."

No 'unrealistic expectations, or unnecessary limitations'

Now 30, Courtney signed off her mountain biking career – at least for now – as cross-country marathon world champion, a title she won in Verbier last year.

The San Francisco native devoted more than two decades of her life to mountain biking, so one might assume the transition away from that community, which has given her so much, would be a wrench for Courtney. However, she takes an entirely different perspective, retaining a fondness for mountain biking but choosing to look at what’s ahead, rather than what’s gone before.

"My husband has often given me the advice that in life you want to move towards things, not away from them. So moving towards something that's really exciting or motivating or where you have a lot to learn is always how I try to make decisions and how I try to structure what I'm working for, and that was certainly the case with the road."

"It's not about leaving mountain biking. I love the discipline. I grew up racing mountain bikes; I've raced mountain bikes my entire life. It's more about following the curiosity and the excitement for something new, which obviously comes with some sacrifices both personally and professionally, making big changes in order to take these next steps in my career."

Managing extreme change can be an even greater mental challenge than a technical one. Courtney comes across as highly confident and self-assured, as though none of this fazes her one bit.

But what if road racing doesn’t work out? Does Courtney’s new set of wheels come with a hint of doubt?

"Being in the team with FDJ, with the performance team we have, with the other riders we have, I really don't feel pressure, and I feel really insulated from that outside doubt," she says.

"For me it's about being in the right environment where I have the opportunity to learn and push myself and test myself, but also be realistic about where I am in the process."

"Inside, I know this is what I want to do. I'm confident in my abilities as an athlete, and I will learn, so there's really no reason to have either unrealistic expectations or unnecessary limitations on what I can achieve."

"I think that the mental side of the sport takes a lot of work and it's a lot of the game, but one of the things that's really fun for me in this period is that it's clear I'm trying something new, it's clear this is my first WorldTour race, and so I feel the freedom to go out and experiment and see where I am, but also know that that's not the final answer, that's actually the starting point."

Riding with purpose for She Sends

Beyond racing, Courtney is a firm believer in the power of cycling and its ability to empower women. She set up the She Sends Foundation in 2023, providing grants and exposure to projects across the USA to promote female participation in mountain biking.

Courtney went a step further in 2025, racing under the She Sends banner with the foundation’s logo emblazoned on her kit. The foundation continues to be a driver for her, but her FDJ United-SUEZ contract means that she can no longer have the logo on show at races. However, her road switch could open up opportunities for the foundation to branch out to the discipline in the future.

"The foundation is still operating in the same way as before, just not on my jersey," Courtney explains.

"I think that there's a huge opportunity to expand the mission and step outside of just off-road racing for the foundation, and in my mind women's cycling is niche enough and being able to be a bit more cross-disciplinary in our initiatives would be really exciting. I also just think it's an amazing moment in women's cycling and I'm hoping that this change will only increase my ability to contribute in the future."

The Foundations gives Courtney a purpose in her racing beyond mere results. Her push for Olympic success is about more than just herself.

"I think having a mission and a purpose behind what you do makes it harder to give up. It makes it a lot more meaningful when it pays off, and I think it also gives you the opportunity to live your values in any moment in sport."

"I think at the end of the day we have a huge opportunity to inspire the next generation, and a responsibility to do so as well."

After several months of Europe ended at the Tour of Britain, Courtney headed home for three weeks for a period of consistent training ahead of the next major step in her road racing experiment.

That next step is a first-time ride at the Road World Championships, her Nationals win earning her automatic selection to the US team and an accelerated chance to take on one of the biggest events of the year. The fast-approaching Worlds in Montreal, Canada, will provide Courtney with yet another 'first' in a year in which everything has changed.

items.title: 'This race was a very good final preparation' – Mathieu van der Poel returns to Luxembourg to build rhythm and form ahead of Road World Championships
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The top favourites for the upcoming Road World Championships in Canada have all taken varied routes to Montreal, with a host of preparation races – including the Vuelta a España, the GPs de Montréal and Québec, and the men's and women's Tours of Britain – to choose from.

Few of the big names have chosen the relatively low-key surroundings of the Tour de Luxembourg for their main build-up race, though 2023 world champion Mathieu van der Poel is heading to one of Europe's smallest countries to put the finishing touches on his Worlds prep.

The five-day ProSeries race doesn't carry a reputation as a key stop en route to the rainbow jersey. However, it does attract several major names each year – including last year's fourth-place finisher in Kigali, Mattias Skjelmose, and Van der Poel himself in 2023, a week before his bronze medal in Zurich.

Speaking ahead of this year's opener, a hilly 157.5km stage, Van der Poel said that he has "good memories" of the race, where he won the opening stage before finishing second overall two years ago.

"I have good memories of the Tour de Luxembourg from two years ago. I won a stage, came close a few more times and finished second overall," he said.

"More importantly, I had a good World Championships in Zurich afterwards, which showed that this race was a very good final preparation."

In the interim, he's been on his mountain bike, racing to second at the UCI World Cup round in Les Gets before taking on the MTB World Championships, where he finished 30th.

Van der Poel said the 701km of racing in Luxembourg this week will help him rediscover the rhythm of road racing ahead of the 273.2km race in Montreal, held on Sunday, September 27.

"I feel it can serve the same purpose this year ahead of the Worlds in Canada. After my mountain bike block, I can definitely use some race rhythm and competitive kilometres on the road. That is the main goal for me here," he said.

Van der Poel is the standout rider on the startlist in Luxembourg. Other notable names lining up for the race include Davide Piganzoli (Visma-Lease a Bike), Tao Geoghegan Hart (Lidl-Trek), Igor Arrieta (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Aurélien Paret-Peintre (Decathlon CMA CGM), and Soudal-QuickStep duo Jasper Stuyven and Dylan van Baarle.

He said he'd be happy to come away from the week with another stage win on the way to Worlds.

"Of course, if there is an opportunity to fight for a stage win, I will take it. A victory would be a nice bonus and could also give me some extra confidence before travelling to Canada."

items.title: Wednesday Posted & Toasted Notes: Emmy Brunson, heated Kolek, no NBA expansion!?
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
You know things are heating up when start getting enough quotes to put together a Bulletin, only I’m keeping those for later this off/preseason.

For now, here’s the latest round of links and notes for you to enjoy as we approach media day about the end of September. Get excited!

  • Knicks Opening Night tickets have exploded in price after the championship, experiencing a silly 526% increase from last season’s home opener.
  • Jalen Brunson made a cameo in Mariska Hargitay’s Emmys cold open.
  • Tyler Kolek is entering Year 3 focused on being more aggressive whenever opportunities come his way, he told The New York Post, and he believes he’s got much more to offer the NBA world: “There’s definitely a lot left [for me to show].”

“I just gotta play my game everyday. Be consistent, whatever the coaches need just follow their direction and let it be what it is.”

  • Kolek echoed his teammates’ broader underdog mentality entering the season even coming off hoisting the Larry O’B. “At this stage, we shouldn’t have to be motivated. We’re champions,” Kolek said. “We know what it looks like, and we’re not just satisfied with one.”
  • Jordan Clarkson keeps openly reminding fans he’s fly.
  • Dirk Nowitzki admitted he never expected Jalen Brunson to develop into a franchise cornerstone in New York. That said, he gave kudos to JB for being “unbelievable on and off the floor” and fully deserving to lead the Knicks to a championship and win Finals MVP.
  • Mitchell Robinson’s move to Boston still stings inside the Knicks’ locker room, with Kolek calling his departure painful. Robinson, meanwhile, says he is entering his Celtics stint with renewed confidence. We’ll see how that goes.

“Right now, I’m just so confident in myself. I feel like this is going to be a great year for me.”

  • Taj Gibson was waived by New Orleans shortly after being acquired from Memphis, then called it a career and joined the Bulls on a coaching role. Also, Taj wants him kid to be like JB.
  • Julius Randle acknowledged returning to New York with Brooklyn feels natural after spending five seasons with the Knicks. “It’s definitely a place that just feels like home,” Randle said.
  • Kawhi Leonard’s trade to Toronto has officially been approved by the league, ending the uncertainty surrounding whether the Raptors would complete the deal after a year-long investigation and its massive aftermath.
  • Speaking of Kawhi, Nikola Jokić said he prefers playing every game rather than managing his workload.
  • Danilo Gallinari also chimed in on the Klaw saga, and blasted the NBA’s punishment of Kawhi Leonard, arguing that Leonard should have faced a much larger financial penalty because of the impact his decisions had on others.

“He should pay all of that $50 million. He changed the trajectory of my career and put me in a difficult situation by sending me away from Los Angeles.

“What happened to my NBA career (when he was traded from the Clippers as part of the SGA-Paul George deal to convince Kawhi to sign with LA) wasn’t decided by a general manager or an owner, but by a player who decided that team wasn’t good enough and wanted something else.”

  • The NBA Board of Governors discussed a possible expansion to Las Vegas and Seattle during meetings in New York on Monday and Tuesday. Commissioner Adam Silver, however, keeps stressing that nothing is guaranteed, with the league still weighing whether to add both cities, one, or neither. Yeah, right?
  • Jalen Duren and Detroit remain far apart on a new contract, with the Pistons’ most recent offer reportedly around five years and $190 million and Duren seeking at least $200 million. The big fella is supposedly seriously considering taking the $9.6 million qualifying offer to reach unrestricted free agency next summer.
  • Team USA won the 2026 FIBA Women’s World Cup by trouncing France 97-79. Breanna Stewart finished with 22 points and 10 rebounds and was named tournament MVP.

items.title: Grand Prix de Wallonie Dames: Karlijn Swinkels launches a long-range sprint to take victory on the Citadelle de Namur
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Karlijn Swinkels (UAE Team L'IMAD) scored a second career victory at the GP de Wallonie Dames, timing her final sprint to perfection at the top of the Citadelle de Namur.

The Dutchwoman's third win of the season – her first since the Trofeo Binda in March – came at the expense of Elisa Balsamo (Lidl-Trek) after the Italian worked to close a gap to Swinkels' teammate Eleonora Gasparrini inside the final 400 metres.

Having followed Balsamo and Célia Gery (FDJ United-SUEZ) across the gap, Swinkels then launched around the outside of the final bend, outpacing Balsamo and Gery to the finish line to take a commanding win.

"Of course, I'm very happy, and I think as a team we were racing really well. Of course, I was a little bit nervous in the final because everyone committed to go again for me today in this final. I'm really happy I could finish the work from the girls off," Swinkels said after the race.

"Actually, I was hoping the final would be a little bit faster. Now, of course, we were going to the finish line with a lot of sprinters. I'm fast, but I didn't expect that I could be faster than Elisa. For this, Gaspa opened the sprint really early, so they had to react. That was when I could come from the back with a bit more speed because last year I made the mistake to come too early and this year I could time it really good.

"It's super special and I really, really wanted to win this race today. Last week was a bit of a difficult week. I'm really happy, and this victory is mostly for my family, my second family in Italy, but also my teammates, who really sacrificed everything for me today."

Earlier in the day, a breakaway of six riders went clear. Marieke Meert (Lotto-Intermarché), Alison Avoine (Ma Petite Enterprise), Camilla Rånes Bye, Viivi Turpeinen (Minimax WB), Rose Kloese (Carbonbike Giordana Sofré by Gen Z), and Zoë van Velzen (WV Schijndel) jumped away after 20km.

They raced away to an advantage of 4:30 at one point as Lidl-Trek and UAE Team L'IMAD took control back in the peloton, though that gap fell to 2:30 as the riders raced into the final 25km.

Movistar also joined in the pacemaking as the peloton slowly reeled in the leading sextet, but the pace wasn't quick enough for some as attacks flew on the Tienne aux Pierres (3.1km at 4.9%) hill 14km from the finish.

With the break in their sights on the way up, a host of riders jumped clear from the peloton. Lauren Dickson (FDJ United-SUEZ) led the new move, taking Gasparrini, defending champion Shari Bossuyt (AG Insurance-Soudal), and Ingvild Gåskjenn (Uno-X Mobility) with her.

The move wouldn't stick to the finish, however, as Lidl-Trek dragged them back into the much-reduced peloton with just over 6km left to ride. The race was then on towards Namur and the famous cobbled ascent to the Citadelle de Namur (3.2km at 4.1%), which would decide the winner.

FDJ led the race onto the climb, setting it up for their leader, 20-year-old French champion Gery. Amber Kraak led the way up the winding road to the Citadelle before pulling off for Dickson to push the pace towards the top.

The British racer held control over the reduced group of no more than 15 as the cobbles turned to tarmac in the final kilometre. Behind, Gasparrini was the first to launch in the final, going with 400 metres to go.

With Balsamo and Gery quick to jump on the Italian's wheel, her attack wasn't the winning move of the day, but it set up her teammate Swinkels, who was sitting in the wheels behind, ready to strike.

Balsamo and Gery had used vital energy in following the move, with Balsamo then hitting the front too early. That left Swinkels in prime position in third wheel, and she was quick to strike, having enough left in the legs to pass Gery and Balsamo around the outside.

items.title: Mads Pedersen helps fund two extra spots for U23 riders in Denmark's World Championships squad
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Denmark originally only had enough money to field four riders in the U23 men's road race, but it has now announced it has been able to fill all six spots.

The change is partly due to "frugal work in the elite sports sector", according to the Danish Cycling Union, but also to a "generous donation" from Denmark's star rider in the elite category.

The funds were always intended to go towards the Danish Cycling Union, and in particular the youth categories, and that has already borne fruit, with Emil Nymand and Kevin Biehl receiving their tickets to Canada.

"I have been working to make this a reality all year, and through frugal work in the elite sports sector and not least a major contribution from Mads Pedersen, it has now succeeded. And that makes me incredibly happy and proud," said national coach Michael Mørkøv.

"These are two riders I have always wanted to have, but budget has previously prevented it. We have now managed to find a solution, and therefore we can expand the squad with Emil Nymand and Kevin Biehl.

"Emil Nymand and Kevin Biehl have both delivered great results in the Giro Next Gen and Giro della Valle d'Aosta, which are among the biggest and most prestigious U23 races. That's why I'm really pleased that we can now give them the opportunity to become part of the World Cup squad.

"I am convinced that it will be of great importance for both riders’ further development and future that they will have the opportunity to ride a world championship. They are both light riders who should be able to do well on the course in Montreal. All in all, it is fantastic news."

items.title: 'I thought we were way past the sexualisation of women in sport' – Demi Vollering and Maddy Nutt among cyclists to hit back at Sydney Sweeney's naked betting advert
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Professional cyclists are among the number of female athletes all over the world who have hit back at a recent advert featuring the US actor Sydney Sweeney, which they say sexualises women’s sport.

Double Tour de France champion Demi Vollering, Olympic track champion Sophie Capewell and gravel pro Maddy Nutt have all commented, saying it undermines progress in normalising women’s sport.

The ad, for a sports betting company, stars Sweeney, showing her naked, barring strategically placed sports equipment. It had huge reach, Sweeney posting some of the ad to her 25 million Instagram followers, and it has since become a major international news story amid criticism from across the sporting world.

"Maybe it’s good that it started a conversation," Vollering wrote in an Instagram post. "But it’s also sad that women still need to have this conversation. For a very long time, women have fought to be seen for what they can DO, not only for how they look.

"And I think many women are simply tired of that. Especially in sport, because sport can teach us something completely different about our bodies. Not: How do I look? But: What can I do?

"And being strong doesn’t make you less feminine. You can race a bike until there is nothing left in your legs and still love putting on a beautiful dress. You can have muscles and feel feminine. You can be powerful and vulnerable."

Capewell spoke to the , saying: "It’s almost like people miss the mark, they don’t fully understand why people are upset about it."

Nutt: 'If this was 20 years ago I wouldn't have been shocked'

Nutt, meanwhile, posted a social media video in which she wrote 'Dear Sydney Sweeney, this is what a female athlete looks like', alongside footage of herself racing and training.

Nutt, who won the Traka 560 and was second at Unbound XL this year, later spoke to about the issue.

"Initially it was just shock seeing it because it was quite distasteful," she said. "I thought we were way past the sexualisation of women in sport, I thought we were at a point where people were starting to really respect female athletes and view women's sport with a much higher level of prestige and appreciation.

"If this was 20 years ago I wouldn't have been shocked. It’s quite a tacky piece of content, and yes, sex sells things, it's a clever advert, and the fact that it's had so much backlash obviously does boost its reach even further.

"But I think from the other side of it, as a female athlete, it's an opportunity to say actually no, this is what women's sport looks like, flip it around and turn it into an opportunity to shout about women's sport and how it has really progressed."

There have been arguments that Sweeney’s ad is no different from any sportswoman who might have posed almost naked, but Nutt sees a crucial difference.

"An athlete showing their athletic body in that way is like a body positivity thing. Showing an athletic body is an empowering thing, whereas this advert was obviously entirely sexual and not an athlete. This is just appealing to that audience who the betting app wants to appeal to."

items.title: 'He's totally disconnected from reality' – Philippe Gilbert slams Tim Wellens' refusal to ride the World Championships for Belgium
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Tim Wellens' decision to skip the UCI Road World Championships has already been heavily debated in Belgium. The dust has still not settled, with fuel being poured on the fire by Philippe Gilbert, who has said that Wellens is "totally disconnected from reality".

The comments, coming from one of the all-time Belgian greats and a former world champion no less, are striking in their strength and directness, with Gilbert accusing Wellens of disloyalty against his country.

Wellens told national coach Serge Pauwels earlier this summer that he would not be available for selection for the Worlds road race in Montreal on September 27, where Remco Evenepoel and Wout van Aert represent a strong hand for the rainbow jersey.

His initial argument was that he was ill after the Tour de France and asked UAE Team Emirates-XRG to skip the Renewi Tour, promising in exchange to absent himself from the Worlds and ride other races for his trade team, including today’s GP de Wallonie.

Wellens’ overall victory at the Tour of Britain earlier this month removed any question marks over his form and threw his decision back into the spotlight. He has since admitted to having second thoughts, especially when Evenepoel reportedly urged him to reconsider, but no real regrets: "10 years ago, I would have done anything to be in the squad. Now I am further along in my career and perhaps have different priorities."

The situation has caused controversy in Belgium and now Gilbert, who won the world title for the country in 2012, has issued a scathing assessment.

"I think you have to be loyal, first and foremost, to your nation. Employers, he has had several, and he will maybe have others before the end of his career, but your nation remains the same. So I think you have to be loyal to your nation, and here he is not, because his arguments don’t hold up."

Gilbert picked up on insinuations in the Belgian media that Wellens, also absent from last year’s Worlds, was reluctant to race against his trade team leader, Tadej Pogačar, who has now been ruled out with an injury. Wellens has not mentioned this as a reason for his absence.

"Even if Pogačar was there, it would not stop him working for a Belgian team that’s in a dream scenario, with two in-form leaders and a route that suits them. I would have dreamt of being part of that adventure,” Gilbert said.

"[His statement] makes no sense, simply. Later, he’ll realise what he’s said and he’ll say ‘that wasn’t the right decision’, because I’m not so sure that he’ll be invited back to the national team so quickly."

items.title: Ben Turner moving on after five years at Ineos – here's how he'll slot right into the QuickStep DNA
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Soudal-QuickStep have announced the signing of British racer Ben Turner on a three-year deal from Netcompany Ineos.

27-year-old Turner, who has raced with Ineos since turning pro in 2022, will boost Soudal-QuickStep's Classics and sprint lineups.

Turner has three professional victories to his name, including sprint wins at the 2025 Vuelta a España and 2025 Tour de Pologne.

He's also been a strong Classics performer, having burst onto the scene in 2022 with top 10 finishes at Dwars door Vlaanderen and Brabantse Pijl plus 11th place at Paris-Roubaix.

"Obviously, for me it's a big privilege to join Soudal-QuickStep, a team which I've always dreamed of being part of since being small and watching the Classics together with my dad," Turner said upon signing with the Belgian team.

"Even after I turned professional, it was a team I was always looking at to see what they were doing in the races and always keeping an eye on them.

"After discussing with Jurgen [Foré, team CEO] and the team, I realised quickly that we are on the same page, that's why I'm super excited to be part of this organisation from 2027. I want to develop myself into a better rider here, try to win races, and help the squad get victories.

"I'm looking forward to being part of this environment and racing for Soudal-QuickStep, it's something that gives me a massive motivation for next season."

Turner is Soudal-QuickStep's third signing for 2027, joining German fastman Tim Torn Teutenberg and Italian all-rounder Lorenzo Milesi on the incoming list. Mikel Landa (Euskaltel-Euskadi) and Casper Pedersen (Uno-X Mobility) are the two riders confirmed to be leaving the team for 2027.

"We have been following Ben for quite some time now and realised that he is the type of rider that would immediately find his place in our team. Ben has the right mindset and character to join the Wolfpack," said Foré.

"He is someone who can perform in the Classics and in stage races, but also help the squad in a wide range of races, and that's why we are excited he will race with us through 2029. We still think he has the capacity to improve even more, and we hope he'll hit new heights in the coming years as part of our squad."

La Vuelta was easily the best Grand Tour of the season, now a wide-open Worlds awaits – Sean Kelly's Vuelta column
items.author: Sean Kelly
items.content:
So much happened at this year's Vuelta a España, and it was such a race that it's hard to know where to start this week's column. But I suppose it should be at the top step of the podium with Enric Mas. The way he rode La Vuelta was unbelievable; he seemed to strike the best vein of form in his life. The Mallorcan looked incredibly controlled on the mountaintop finishes, taking time when he needed to across the second half of the race. We always talk about Movistar and that they can be a disaster of a team at times, but my God, once they got the red jersey within their ranks, the whole team stepped up and performed differently.

I think Mas' victory will definitely give them a kick up the backside as a team. The sports directors will be saying, 'this is what we should have been doing for the last couple of years' – they've been in a bit of a drought since Alejandro Valverde left, and although they have the riders, they just haven't been getting the results they should have been. Of course, Mas himself has had tricky periods, with his injury and operation, but when you see what they're capable of at this Vuelta, then you have to ask, where was that before?

Of course, the one caveat there is Tadej Pogačar. Had he not crashed out at the end of the first week, he would have likely won, considering the lead he'd already built up. Yet, given the way the final stages were ridden, and factoring in potential fatigue towards the end of the Slovenian's second consecutive Grand Tour, I feel like it might have been more open than we anticipated. It's worth remembering too that Pogačar struggled during the final week of last year's Tour; his team said he was sick, but how unwell actually was he? UAE Team Emirates-XRG know rival teams will analyse his performances for any weaknesses, so perhaps illness is an easy way to cover up any repeated Grand Tour fatigue that might plague Pogačar in the final days of a three-week race.

Nonetheless, I think for cycling, and for the real cycling followers that know about bike racing, La Vuelta was easily the best Grand Tour of the season by far – there were so many days where we had no idea what the outcome of the stage would be.

Another top performer in this La Vuelta was hands down Matthew Brennan, not just because he won five stages, but because of how he rode this Grand Tour, the first of his professional career. He was without a doubt the fastest rider at this year's race, with an honourable mention for XDS Astana's Alessandro Romele, who looks like a rider who's going to do a lot in the future. It was an absolute dream Vuelta for Visma-Lease a Bike's young British talent, though, and the question is: what will he target next year?

It will be fascinating when he comes up against the likes of Tim Merlier and other real fast men like Jonathan Milan and Mads Pedersen. He can get over a lot of small climbs, and given how crazy organisers are with stage routes now, Brennan will chalk up plenty of stage race wins. I know he's open to racing the Tour next year, especially because it starts in the UK. Naturally, though, competition is incredibly high for Visma-Lease a Bike's Tour de France squad, especially when you consider their yellow jersey ambitions and the multi-faceted role that Wout van Aert plays in the squad.

A wide-open World Championships

Speaking of the Belgian, he was equally impressive at this year's La Vuelta, serving as a lead-out man for Brennan, but also scoring two victories of his own and the green jersey. Of course, he didn't race the Tour, so he's getting into form later in the season, and has a level of freshness that should give him and his Belgian World Championships squad a very good chance in Canada. They just need to get organised and avoid any tactical problems between Van Aert and Evenepoel.

It's going to be a very interesting Road World Championships because with no Pogačar, there's a void that needs to be filled. When Pogačar is in a one-day Classic like the Worlds, it's like watching spaghetti boil. You know what's about to happen; you just have to be ready when the moment arrives. In the past, the Slovenian would just use his team to put everybody on the limit and then attack at a certain point, be it 40km or 50km to go, leaving the rest of the field in indecision as they question whether to chase him down or turn their attention to the podium places.

I think Remco Evenepoel will think about using the same tactic, but will he be good enough to make it stick? If he doesn't, then it could well be Wout van Aert who finds himself in a move, and the Belgian squad's strategy changes. It's going to be fascinating to see who can capitalise on the Pogačar-shaped hole in Montréal at the end of this month.

items.title: 'The big guys usually fighting for the podium are now going for the win' – British riders look to capitalise on absence of Pogačar at Worlds in support of 'genuine contender' Tom Pidcock
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Half of the British team for the elite men's road race have just finished the Vuelta a España, and will be looking to carry their form through to the road Montreal World Championships in Canada and provide support for a "genuine contender for the win" in leader Tom Pidcock.

Making up the Scottish contingent will be Vuelta Best Young Rider and sixth-place finisher Oscar Onley, and time trial breakthrough rider Callum Thornley, with the former racing his third elite Worlds RR in a row and the latter making his debut.

Both are confident with Pidcock among their ranks, but for Onley, after a gritty performance in Spain, he will be racing just his first one-day race of the 2026 season. His previous best result is from Zurich in 2024, when he was 16th as GB's top finisher.

"Well, I'm hoping that three weeks riding around Spain is good training for Worlds," Onley told in Granada after stage 21.

"I'm hoping I come out of this in good shape, recover quite well, and then I think in the road race we have a really exciting opportunity as the GB team with Tom [Pidcock] and [Adam]. I hope to be there deep in the final as well to really support those guys."

For his fellow Scot Thornley, it was a surprise to be included in the team as the only rider doing both the time trial, on September 20, and the road race a week later. But given his runner-up finish behind only Stefan Küng on stage 18 of the Vuelta against the clock, he's got the form to put in a solid performance alongside Ethan Hayter.

"I'm doing the TT and the road race, so that's the next target. I'm really, really happy with that, super excited to travel on Wednesday for the TT," he told last Sunday.

"I never thought at the start of the year that the Worlds TT would be a goal, but now it is, and I'm going there, and I'll aim high and try and get a medal. I'm super excited."

Aside from excelling in the TT, Thornley had also been part of the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team supporting Primož Roglič in his GC bid at the Vuelta, eventually finishing second behind Enric Mas. It's an experience he described as unforgettable on debut.

"It really is surreal. Every day when they introduce him to all the fans on the podium, the applause he gets is like quite similar to when a goal is scored in a football stadium," said the 23-year-old. "It's been an honour, and I think I'll remember forever that my first Grand Tour was riding for Primož Roglič."

The same will be true of Worlds, with the Slovenian unable to recover in time: with him out, it puts the likes of Great Britain more in the running for the rainbow jersey, when it originally looked almost a given that Pogačar would win his third world title in a row.

"I think it's kind of like an unspoken thing. Everyone is now aware that it's a very open race and there's a lot of people who can win, but it's not really something that's talked about," said Thornley.

"But I think for sure, all those big guys who would usually be fighting for the podium are now fighting for the win, and I'm sure it makes it even more at stake than normal, really."

"And for us, it'll be cool. Especially racing with Tom because he's really a genuine contender to win, and the rest of the team is also super strong. I'm excited to race with my fellow countrymen and just be all in for one goal, so I'm super positive to be a part of the elite Worlds for the first time."

Alongside Onley and Thornley heading from the Vuelta to Worlds for Great Britain are James Shaw and Finlay Pickering, with Pidcock, Yates, Fred Wright, and Mark Donovan making up the rest of the eight-man squad for the road race on September 27.

items.title: Knicks sign John Konchar and Drew Eubanks to training camp deals
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
In a league where everyone seems to have lost their minds, the Knicks have had a quiet offseason. I mean, after you win a championship, why be overtly active when you have everything you need to go back-to-back?

We haven’t heard of a real roster move since the attempt to sign Mavericks center Moussa Cisse to an offer sheet back on July 19, but as training camp approaches in the next few weeks, the Knicks need to figure out who’s filling the final roster spots.

Two of those names who will be competing for that spot will be former Grizzlies wing John Konchar and former Kings forward Drew Eubanks, who were both signed on Tuesday night.

Konchar, an undrafted free agent out of Purdue-Fort Wayne in 2019, grew from a little-used role player into a key contributor for several years in Memphis. He played just 62 games in his first two seasons, but began to become a serious member of the rotation in 2021-22.

Across the next three seasons, Konchar averaged 4.8 points, 4.5 rebounds, and 1.6 assists on 45.7% from the field and 35.5% from three in 199 games (53 starts) for a turbulent team that went from being one of the league’s youngest and brightest to most disappointing. He never played nor contributed much when the playoffs came around, but was soli regular season depth.

He began to be phased out of the rotation in 2024-25, playing just 46 games without any long-term injuries. A sharp regression from downtown (28.4% in 2025-26) made him expendable, leading to him being sent to Utah as part of the Jaren Jackson Jr. trade as expiring salary, where he played out the rest of the season with a crummy, tanking Jazz team.

When things are going right for Konchar, the 6’5” wing plays a lot taller than his height, averaging 8.2 rebounds per 36 with two stocks (steals+blocks). He’s had stretches where he can be a real sniper, shooting over 37% from three on three different occasions, but is also extremely streaky, having shot sub-34% also in three different seasons.

As for Eubanks, affectionately nicknamed the “Michael Jordan of Troutdale, Oregon”, he signed as an undrafted free agent out of Oregon State in 2018 with the San Antonio Spurs, playing 3.5 years as a solid bench player for a transitional era in Spurs basketball before being traded to the Raptors at the 2022 trade deadline for Goran Dragic and a first-round pick, eventually being bought out.

Since then, he’s shuffled around the league. He played the best basketball of his career in 22 games as a starter for the Portland Trail Blazers in late 2022, averaging 14.5 points and 8.5 rebounds, but reverted to the regular role player he’s always been the following year.

He’s played for four different teams over the last three years, making stops in Phoenix, LA (Clippers), Utah, and Sacramento, where he played 42 games last season. In his eight-year career, he’s averaged 5.6 points and 4.3 rebounds on 60.3% from the field.

Now, it’s extremely unlikely that these two players will both make the Opening Night roster, as the Knicks are currently unable to sign two players to standard contracts without exceeding the second apron. It seems like these two will be among the players competing for just one roster spot, with the 6’10” Eubanks likely being the favorite… or is he?

We haven’t gotten the financials, but Konchar is a guy who reportedly got interest from Miami, Orlando, and Toronto. As Ian Begley put it shortly after signing, he likely would not have signed here if he didn’t see a real path towards making the roster, something that the front office would have had to assure him of given the situation.

Could this be the precursor to a trade? Even if nothing is imminent, is this a sign that the Knicks are more willing to trade someone (Deuce McBride?) for a center during training camp?

The Knicks are currently at just 17 players on their training camp roster, with 13 standard deals, these two, Liam Robbins (signed to an Exhibit 10), and Tyler Nickel (likely to be signed to a two-way). They can sign four more.

items.title: Taj Gibson announces retirement, joins Bulls coaching staff
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
The second-oldest active player in basketball is no more, as OAKAAK Taj Gibson announced his retirement on Monday afternoon following his release by the New Orleans Pelicans last week. He will join the Chicago Bulls’ coaching staff under Tiago Splitter for 2026-27.

Gibson, a Brooklyn native, was selected No. 26 overall by the Bulls in 2009 out of USC. It was with Chicago that he spent the bulk of his career, debuting as an extremely old rookie at the age of 24 and growing into one of the best backup power forwards in the game.

He finished fifth in Rookie of the Year voting in 2010, fifth in Sixth Man of the Year voting in 2012, and had the best season of his career in 2013-14, where he played all 82 games and averaged 13 points, 6.8 rebounds, and 1.4 blocks in a bench role, finishing as an extremely close runner-up to Jamal Crawford for Sixth Man of the Year.

It was in Chicago that he grew close to head coach Tom Thibodeau, a connection that would pay dividends down the road. Thibs coached the Bulls from 2010-15.

Shortly after he was canned, Gibson left Chicago as the Bulls entered a rebuild. He was traded to Oklahoma City in February 2017 with Doug McDermott and a 2018 2nd for Cam Payne, Anthony Morrow, and Joffrey Lauvergne. An interesting fact here: McDermott and the Bulls’ 2018 2nd would be flipped a few months later to the Knicks for Carmelo Anthony, and that 2nd became Mitchell Robinson.

He’d slide in next to Steven Adams as the Thunder’s starting power forward for the rest of the 2016-17 season in the first year of the post-KD era, but left in the offseason when Thibs’ new team in Minnesota came calling with a two-year, $28 million pact.

It was there that Taj emerged as a full-time starter as a grizzled veteran, posting 11.5 points and 6.9 rebounds across 153 games as a Timberwolf, but when Thibs was canned, he was out the door as well.

The most relevant chapter of his career to us came when he inked a two-year, $20 million contract with the Knicks in 2019 as part of the “four PFs” offseason in the aftermath of the KD/Kyrie disaster. David Fizdale and Mike Miller would utilize the 34-year-old as more of a center for the first time in his career, using him as a mentor for Robinson. He’d play just 16.5 minutes a game, but started 56 of the 62 games he played as a shield for a young and erratic Robinson’s foul trouble.

His team option was declined for 2020-21, but we should’ve read the tea leaves as soon as Thibodeau was hired as coach that summer. After the Nova Knick 1.0 prototype (Omari Spellman) fizzled out in the first week of January, Gibson returned to fill out the depth chart behind Robinson and Nerlens Noel.

This year marked the backstretch of Gibson’s career, where his experience and mentality were significantly more valuable than his on-court contributions. He would grow into a solid role off the bench, particularly when Robinson was injured.

With the Knicks surprisingly competitive, we suddenly saw the 35-year-old put into the spotlight when Robinson was ruled out for the season, and both he and Noel were stuck as overmatched bigs against Clint Capela and the Hawks. Of the 20 career playoff starts he had, three of them came in that first round series.

He was re-signed for 2021-22 and played a similar role, this time being forced to step up into a backup role due to Noel’s long-term injury. In a frustrating season for the team, he showed a new, interesting wrinkle to his game: shooting threes.

It looked like his time in New York was over when he signed with the Wizards in 2022-23, where he played 49 games as a vet for a very young and bad team, but he’d get one more chance to play for his hometown soon enough. When Robinson suffered a seemingly season-ending ankle injury in December 2023, it was Gibson who got a non-guaranteed contract to fill his shoes.

He’d be yo-yo’d around for the rest of the year, being released in mid-January to avoid guaranteeing his contract before inking a pair of 10-day contracts later in the season, but with Robinson’s unlikely return nearing ahead of the playoffs, Gibson played his final game as a Knick on February 14, 2024, going scoreless in nine minutes.

He finished his Knicks career averaging 4.9 points and 4.4 rebounds on 56.7% from the field in 175 games (64 starts) across four seasons. From there, he continued to be the token veteran on bad teams, playing four games in March 2024 for Detroit before signing one-year deals in both Charlotte and Memphis.

He hangs it up after playing 10 games for the Grizzlies down the stretch in 2025-26 before being traded in the Jordan Hawkins deal to the Pels, who subsequently waived him.

Gibson’s spot in Knicks lore is not that of someone who had an iconic moment that will be replayed forever, but as someone who was there as a transitional piece from the bad times to the bright times. Playing for the team he likely dreamed of playing for growing up, he transitioned from a starting-caliber forward to an end-of-roster veteran, providing depth and experience.

People forget this, but Gibson is the only player aside from Julius Randle and Mitchell Robinson whose Knicks career spanned from David Fizdale to the year 2024. He was there for LolKnicks, the We Here season, and (very briefly) the Brunson revival. Championships are not entirely built by the stars that finished the job, they’re fortified by players who built the foundation.

Maybe Gibson wasn’t a true foundational piece of the rise from irrelevance to competence, but he was a constant throughout it. It’s a great hire for a young Bulls team under an inexperienced head coach in Splitter.

items.title: Haaland goal should not have stood but VAR made the right call with Sunderland penalty | Chris Foy

Matt Donohue is only human and made a mistake, but, in general, referees have started well this season

There was a disappointing outcome on a big decision in the Manchester derby and no one will feel it more than the video assistant referee, Matt Donohue. On Sunday night, Pro Ref confirmed that Donohue had made a mistake in allowing Erling Haaland’s goal in City’s 1-0 victory to stand when Enzo Fernández had been in an offside position.

When a VAR considers a decision such as this they start from the point at which the goal is scored and work backwards. Here, when Haaland scores, the flag is raised by the assistant referee for offside. The VAR automatically checked that on-field decision and used a semi‑automated system to show Haaland was onside. items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Controversy rules the Manchester derby, Coventry are dunked on and Tottenham still can’t score a goal

The 199th Manchester derby was defined by two refereeing decisions: Phil Foden’s first-half red card for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes, and the intervention by the video assistant referee to award Erling Haaland’s winning goal despite Enzo Fernández appearing to interfere with play from an offside position. In both cases, a healthy dose of common sense might have led to a different outcome and Pro Ref admitted that Haaland’s goal should not have stood. Still, it is tough to argue that the final result was harsh on United. Foden’s dismissal gave the hosts a huge opportunity they failed to take, their best chance falling to Bryan Mbeumo in stoppage time. Michael Carrick began his reign with a 2-0 home derby win against 11 men in January, so this felt like a backward step for the manager, unable to find a way to control the game. Carrick also bemoaned City’s two days of extra rest after Champions League games, but chose to keep Fernandes and others on for 90 minutes in the 4-0 stroll past Sabah. United’s next two league games are away at Fulham and at home to Spurs. Carrick will need to be smarter to stop an early-season wobble becoming something more serious.

items.title: Knicks sign Milicic to Exhibit 10 contract. No, not that Milicic
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
As we near training camp and the preseason, the New York Knicks are starting to fill out their roster, with more than several slots and opportunities still available behind the defending NBA champions’ established rotation.

On Saturday, a familiar name entered the Knicks realm when, out of the blue, we read the name “Milicic” linked to the New York franchise.

Only, you know, not Milicic.

Polish outlet Interia Sport’s Karol Wasiek reported that free agent forward Igor Milicic Jr., no relation to Serbian native Darko, agreed to an Exhibit 10 contract with the Knicks, allowing the 24-year-old to compete for a roster spot or a two-way deal during the upcoming camp.

“@SportINTERIA has established that Igor Milicić Jr. is the next Pole with an NBA contract. According to our information, the basketball player has signed an exhibit-10 type contract with the New York Knicks.” — Karol Wasiek

The 6-foot-10, 225-pound forward went undrafted in 2025 following a four-year college career that included stops at Virginia (16 games), Charlotte (66) and Tennessee (37). Milicic averaged 9.4 points, 6.7 rebounds and 1.9 assists across 37 starts during his final college season with the Volunteers.

That said, Igor’s best amateur season came a year earlier when he put up a 13-8-2 stat line shooting 48.7% from the field and 37.6% from three with the 49ers.

Milicic spent last season with the Delaware Blue Coats, the Philadelphia 76ers’ G League affiliate. He averaged 6.9 points, 5.0 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 18.8 minutes across 45 appearances.

The Polish lad also played seven Summer League games with the San Antonio Spurs this offseason, and the truth is that his age, size, and positional flexibility should give him an opportunity to compete for a place within New York’s organization, whether that’s in the majors (more than unlikely) or the minors (slightly less likely).

The Knicks currently have all three two-way contract slots available. According to Wasiek, all those openings factored heavily into Milicic’s decision to join New York, hoping to snatch one of them along with the developmental opportunity the Knicks offered him.

For context, an Exhibit 10 contract can be converted into a two-way deal, and Milicic could also receive a bonus of up to approximately $91,000 if New York waives him before the regular season and he subsequently spends at least 60 days with the Westchester Knicks.

items.title: Knicks face tough Miles McBride decision after latest contract-talks update
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Miles “Deuce” McBride enters the 2026-27 season as the longest-tenured New York Knicks player following Mitchell Robinson’s exit and he’s surely turned into an important contributor for the reigning champs after averaging a career-high 12.0 points while shooting 41.3% from three last season.

According to SNY’s Ian Begley, the Knicks and McBride’s representatives have remained in regular contact, but New York’s financial situation could make a long-term extension difficult.

“This one is tricky because Miles McBride has definitely earned a raise,” Begley reported. “He’s outplayed his contract (3 years, $13 million) by a significant amount.”

McBride is entering the final season of that contract. Begley noted Knicks owner James Dolan’s mandate not to exceed the NBA’s $221 million second apron this season as the major roadblock for reaching such an agreement.

Potential extensions for Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart and eventually Jalen Brunson will inevitably increase the money committed to New York’s starting lineup, and McBride looks like the one set to absorb most of the collateral damage — assuming all parties find a way for him to stay.

“So there isn’t much financial wiggle room for a McBride extension,” Begley reported.

In a promising updated and despite the constraints, neither side has given up on the possibility of extending their relationship.

“In a perfect world, those conversations would produce a multi-year extension for McBride,” Begley reported. “The longest-tenured Knick, McBride loves New York, loves his teammates; he was an integral part of this team’s rise.”

We all know the alternative, as harsh and hard to stomach it might be: trading Deuce before next year’s deadline. That said, there’s no doubt McBride is one of (if not the absolute best) the lague’s most valuable sixth-man trade chips and would attract significant interest from other teams.

“We’re certainly not there yet,” Begley reported. “But logic tells you that’s where things could be headed.”

For now, McBride is set to enter the season with New York with one year left on his deal and a date we’ll all remember no matter what ends up happening circled in his calendar: ring night in late-October.

items.title: Record Watch: Five Knicks benchmarks in jeopardy this season
items.author: John Gove
items.content:
Defending a championship changes the vibe during regular-season play. When the goal is to repeat a championship in June, Tuesday night games in February can feel like a formality. Nobody wants to overexert a key player in a meaningless game on the off chance that he’ll blow a hammy. However, Mike Brown’s offense, built for another deep playoff run, can’t help but generate eye-popping stats all season long.

Between the exploding scoreboards, higher possession counts, and New York’s elite playmakers and scorers, several Knicks records are suddenly at risk. Some of these benchmarks have survived nearly 40 years, while the ink for others is still wet in the books. A closer look at the roster and statistics suggests five specific franchise records could realistically fall this season. Let’s dive in.

Single-Season 30-Point Games

  • Current Record: 36 games – Richie Guerin (1961-1962), Patrick Ewing (1989-90), Jalen Brunson (2023-24)
  • 2026-27 Season Target: 37 games

The current franchise mark for the most 30-point contest in a regular season is a three-way tie spanning three distinct eras of Knicks basketball. Richie Guerin established the benchmark during the fast-break pace of the early 1960s. Patrick Ewing matched it during his prime, dominating the post game-in and game-out while carrying the team on his broad shoulders and aching knees. Captain Jalen Brunson joined the two Hall of Famers two seasons ago during his rise to All-NBA status.

Of every record on this list, this one is the most wobbly. Brunson remains the undisputed engine of New York’s half-court offense, combining incredible footwork with elite basketball smarts.

In Mike Brown’s five-out system, defenses can no longer load up in the paint without leaving deadly perimeter shooters uncovered. Having Karl-Anthony Towns at center pulls defensive anchors 25 feet away from the basket, giving Brunson wider driving lanes, fewer double-teams, and access to his mid-range spots. Assuming he’ll be healthy all season (knock on wood and cross yourself), Brunson claiming sole possession of this record with 37-plus 30-point games feels more like a matter of when, not if.

Single-Game Scoring Record

  • Current Record: 62 points – Carmelo Anthony (January 24, 2014 vs. Charlotte Bobcats)
  • 2026-27 Season Target: 63 points

First, a moment of silence for the Charlotte Bobcats. . . . Okay, we’re good to go.

Carmelo Anthony’s 62-point masterclass against Charlotte has stood untouched for 13 years. In a legendary isolation clinic, Melo shot 23-of-35 from the floor without recording a single assist or turnover. Surpassing a single-game point total like that requires the blend of crazy shot volume, incredible efficiency, (no small degree of selfishness,) and a game that’s competitive enough to keep starters on the floor late into the fourth quarter.

New York’s current roster is different because it features distinct creators who can completely go off in a single game. Brunson already came within a single point of the record, dropping 61 points on 47 shot attempts against the Spurs in March 2024. Meanwhile, Towns brings a personal career-high of 62 points from his time in Minnesota, with an outside stroke that can cause box score chaos. If Towns hits six or seven early threes while dominating the glass, or if Brunson takes over a high-paced track meet, Carmelo’s iconic record could melt like a stick of butter on a sunny afternoon.

Single Season Team 3-Pointers

  • Current Record: 1,168 made three-pointers (2025-26)
  • 2026-27 Season Target: 1,169 made three-pointers

New York set a new record last season, draining 1,168 three-pointers. And Mike Brown’s Knicks are just getting started.

Brown’s scheme relies heavily on five-out principles that are designed to distort perimeter coverage. With movement shooters on the bench (Shamet, McBride, and occasionally Alvarado and Clarkson), the sheer volume of perimeter attempts is bound to increase. Averaging roughly 14 made threes a game across a full schedule, and thereby breaking their own team record for a second straight season, seems like the natural trajectory for this squad.

Individual Single Season 3-Pointers

  • Current Record: 283 made three-pointers – Donte DiVincenzo (2023-24 season)
  • 2026-27 Season Target: 284 made three-pointers

When Donte DiVincenzo poured in 283 three-pointers during his lone full season with the Knicks, he shattered Evan Fournier’s previous mark of 241, setting an incredible bar for perimeter volume. Reaching that total requires a player to average roughly 3.5 made threes per game while appearing in almost every matchup.

DiVincenzo and Fournier are long gone, but the team has redistributed the heavy perimeter workload across its primary offensive tools. Both Towns and Brunson shoot near 40% from beyond the arc and often get the green light in Brown’s system. If KAT maintains a high-volume, trailing-center role in transition, or if Cap takes even more off-dribble pull-up jumpers, DiVo’s record could easily be squashed before the season’s end.

Single Season Point Total

  • Current Record: 2,347 points – Patrick Ewing (1989-90 season)
  • 2026-27 Season Target: 2,348 points

Ewing’s 1989-90 campaign remains the ultimate test of single-season scoring in franchise history. Piling up 2,347 total points, Ewing averaged 28.6 points per contest and played all 82 games. Obviously, the big fella served as the team’s primary generator and carried most of the load that year.

Surpassing Ewing’s record is hands-down the most grueling challenge on this list of beatable benchmarks. Per-game averages mean little if a player misses games due to load management or minor injury, so any absence from the floor will interrupt the scoring pace needed to top Patrick.

Across 77 appearances in 2023-24, Brunson recorded 2,212 points, which put him within spitting distance of the record. To beat out Ewing, Jalen would need to maintain a scoring average north of 28 points per game, while playing in at least 80 contests. Requiring a combination of elite offensive production and availability, the 2,348 points in a season is the hardest to crack, and as Jalen enters his thirties, Coach Brown is likely to play Jalen for shorter stints in unimportant games, to preserve him for the offseason. Still, it is mathematically within reach.

Some franchise records are so incredible that they’re unlikely to be toppled, given the changes in play-style, rules, and rosters over time. However, Mike Brown’s team, based on a high-volume, high-efficiency attack, is not your father’s Knicks. In the 1995-96 season, the ‘Bockers averaged 97.2 points per game and attempted 1,285 three-pointers; thirty years later, they averaged 116.5 PPG and took 3,133 threes. And that’s not even top-five in the league! (The Warriors tried 3,616.) With the firepower currently employed at MSG, some of these historical benchmarks are truly at risk.

Which records do you think will fall this year? Talk about it below!

items.title: Knicks’ interest in veteran free-agent center emerges ahead of training camp
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The New York Knicks have Karl-Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond positioned atop their center depth chart, but the defending champions remain without a traditional third center as training camp approaches and this saga doesn’t feel any closer to an end.

In yet another update on the situation, according to SNY’s Ian Begley, veteran free agent Tony Bradley has emerged on the Knicks’ radar as New York continues evaluating potential additions for its remaining roster spots, with a competition for those expected to take place throughout camp and the preseason.

“One other note on free agent signings ahead of training camp: veteran center Tony Bradley has also been a player on the Knicks’ radar,” Begley reported.

If you’re like me, you probably though Bradley was 35 already. Turns out he’s only 28!

Even then, and while Bradley would provide an experienced third option behind Towns and Drummond, don’t expect TB (or whoever ends up landing in New York) to find a clear and open path into coach Mike Brown’s established rotation.

Begley noted that the Knicks are comfortable with their current top two options despite the absence of another traditional center, making it even tougher for Mystery Man to get any potential playing time.

“The Knicks do not currently have a third center, but there is a strong degree of confidence internally in the Karl-Anthony Towns-Andre Drummond duo at the position,” Begley reported.

Bradley spent last season with the Indiana Pacers and Atlanta Hawks, appearing in 41 games and averaging 4.0 points and 2.8 rebounds in 11 minutes per game.

The 6-foot-10 center has eight seasons of NBA experience after entering the league as the No. 28 overall pick in the 2017 NBA Draft. Bradley owns career averages of 4.3 points and 3.8 rebounds in 234 regular-season appearances.

Begley previously reported that New York has also shown interest in free agents Drew Eubanks and John Konchar while evaluating its remaining roster openings, hinting at the openness of the Knicks’ brass to land a variety of player types ahead of their title defense.

For now, the Knicks’ next step is opening training camp before they face the Philadelphia 76ers in the first game of the preseason.
